title: Structuring Results for Analysis
text:
This section of the user guide focuses on data visualization in LISSY using Stata. Beyond general plotting practices, we highlight a few particularities that users should be aware of when working in the LISSY environment, things that wouldn’t arise when coding locally. Our focus is exclusively on trends (line charts), organized around six templates that users can adapt to their own countries and variables of interest.
Working from templates matters more here than it would in a local session. LISSY operates on a job-submission system rather than an interactive one: there is no way to inspect intermediate output or tweak a chart on the fly, and every change requires a new submission. Starting from a tested example that already matches your use case significantly reduces the number of iterations needed.
Each template addresses a different combination of practical dimensions: the number of countries, the type of variable being plotted (a flow variable or a categorical one), the level of disaggregation, and the number of indicators shown simultaneously. Together they cover most situations a user is likely to encounter.
The six examples are organized as follows:


Examples 1–2 — single variable, one country or multiple countries (flow variable; categorical variable)

Examples 3–4 — categorical variable across multiple countries, with increasing disaggregation (standardized variable; country-specific variable)

Example 5 — standardized disaggregation by a person-level variable, multiple countries side by side

Example 6 — multiple derived indicators in a single plot, single country







Important



All examples use graph export to save the chart as a .png file. This is not optional in LISSY: without an export command, no chart is returned. When submitting multiple figures in a single job, each must be given a unique filename — reusing the same name will silently overwrite earlier outputs and only the last chart will be retrievable.




This first template computes median equivalised disposable household income (dhi) over time for several countries simultaneously, expressed in PPP-adjusted 2021 US dollars. It illustrates the most common pattern: a flow variable, aggregated to a single statistic per country-year, plotted as connected lines.
A few aspects of the code are worth noting. The loop over dname processes each country-wave separately before appending results to a temporary file — this is the standard LISSY pattern for cross-wave computations that need to be done at the dataset level (here, IQR capping and percentile estimation). The twoway command is then built dynamically by looping over countries, so the code scales to any number of countries without manual adjustment.

    // Import data 

lissyuse, iso2(fr lu se us uk) hvars(hid cname year dhi nhhmem hwgt dname) from(2010) to(2024)
qui merge m:1 cname year  using "$myincl/ppp_2021.dta" ,  keep(match)

    // Loop over each dataset

tempfile final
save `final', replace emptyok
qui levelsof dname, local(levels)
foreach ccyy of local levels {
    preserve
    keep if dname == "`ccyy'"
    drop if missing(dhi)
    * Person weight
    generate double pwt = hwgt * nhhmem
    * IQR capping (done per ccyy)
    generate double dhi_log = log(dhi)
    replace dhi_log = 0 if dhi_log == . & dhi != .
    sort dhi_log hwgt
    qui percentils dhi_log [aw = hwgt], p(25 75)
    local p75 = e(Perc_75)
    local p25 = e(Perc_25)
    gen double iqr     = `p75' - `p25'
    gen double upper_bound = `p75' + (iqr * 3)
    gen double lower_bound = `p25' - (iqr * 3)
    replace dhi = exp(upper_bound) if dhi > exp(upper_bound)
    replace dhi = exp(lower_bound) if dhi < exp(lower_bound)
    * Equivalisation
    generate double ey = dhi / (nhhmem^0.5)
    * PPP adjustment
    generate double ey_adj = ey / lisppp
    * Median
    sort ey_adj hwgt
    qui percentils ey_adj [aw = pwt], p(50)
    gen median = e(Perc_50)
    collapse median, by(cname year dname)
    * Append to final file
    append using `final'
    save `final', replace
    restore
}
use `final', clear
drop if missing(median)
keep cname year dname median
* Build twoway command dynamically
qui levelsof cname, local(countries)
local twoway_cmd ""
local i 1
foreach c of local countries {
    local twoway_cmd `"`twoway_cmd' (connected median year if cname == "`c'", msize(small))"'
    local labels `"`labels' lab(`i' "`c'")"'
    local i = `i' + 1
}

    // Plotting 

twoway `twoway_cmd', ///
    ytitle("") xtitle("") ///
    ylabel(0(10000)60000, angle(horizontal) labsize(vsmall) format(%8.0gc)) ///
    xlabel(, labsize(vsmall)) ///
    title("Median Disposable Household Income in US int.$ 2021", size(small)) ///
    caption("LIS - Luxembourg Income Study", size(tiny) position(5)) ///
    graphr(color(white)) ///
    legend(pos(3) col(1) size(vsmall) `labels')

graph export "$mypdf/ex1.png", replace width(871) height(522)




This template shifts from a flow variable to a categorical one. It plots the share of employment by industry sector (indb1) in Germany over time, using relative frequencies rather than a monetary aggregate. The structure is similar to Example 1 — a dynamic twoway loop over categories — but the data preparation is simpler: a collapse on weighted counts followed by a within-wave normalization is sufficient.
This is a useful template for any LIS variable that takes a small number of discrete values and for which tracking compositional change over time is of interest (employment type, household structure, education level, etc.).






Note



Variable availability: Industry of employment is not available for all country-waves in LIS. Before running this template on a new country, check coverage in the LIS variable documentation, or using the methods described in the early chapters of this guide.



lissyuse, iso2(de) hvars(hid cname year nhhmem dname) pvars(pid indb1 ppopwgt) from(2010) to(2024) 


drop if missing(indb1)  

collapse (sum) ppopwgt, by(dname indb1 cname year) 
    bysort dname: egen total = total(ppopwgt) 
    gen percent = ppopwgt / total * 100 


gen short_label = "" 
    replace short_label = "Agriculture"    if indb1 == 1 
    replace short_label = "Manufacturing"  if indb1 == 2 
    replace short_label = "Construction"   if indb1 == 3 
    replace short_label = "Trade"          if indb1 == 4 
    replace short_label = "Transport"      if indb1 == 5 
    replace short_label = "Finance"        if indb1 == 6 
    replace short_label = "Real estate"    if indb1 == 7 
    replace short_label = "Public admin"   if indb1 == 8 
    replace short_label = "Other services" if indb1 == 9 

qui levelsof indb1, local(codes) 
local twoway_cmd "" 
local labels "" 
local i 1 
foreach c of local codes { 
    qui levelsof short_label if indb1 == `c', local(lbl) clean 
    local twoway_cmd `"`twoway_cmd' (connected percent year if indb1 == `c', msize(small) lwidth(medthick))"' 
    local labels `"`labels' lab(`i' "`lbl'")"' 
    local i = `i' + 1 
} 


twoway `twoway_cmd', /// 
    ytitle("") xtitle("") /// 
    ylabel(, angle(horizontal) labsize(vsmall) format(%5.1f)) /// 
    xlabel(, labsize(vsmall)) /// 
    title("Employment by Industry Sector, Germany", size(small)) /// 
    caption("LIS - Luxembourg Income Study", size(tiny) position(5)) /// 
    graphr(color(white)) /// 
    legend(pos(3) col(1) size(vsmall) `labels')  

graph export "$mypdf/ex2.png", replace width(871) height(522)








Tip



The short labels assigned manually via replace short_label = ... are necessary because indb1 is stored as a numeric code. An alternative is to use decode indb1, gen(indb1_label) and then strip the numeric prefix from the value label. This is the approach used in Example 3.




This template extends Example 2 to multiple countries, using occupation group (occa1) rather than industry. Because a single twoway plot with all countries and categories at once would be illegible, each country gets its own subplot, which are then assembled side by side using graph combine.
The label extraction here uses decode followed by regex parsing to separate the numeric code from the value label text — a cleaner approach than manual reassignment when the number of categories is large.






Note



graph combine as a faceting tool: we generate one named graph per country with name(g_i’, replace)and then we combine them side by side via the optioncols()` which controls the grid layout.



lissyuse, iso2(pe lu) pvars(pid occa1 ppopwgt) hvars(hid cname year dname) from(2000) to(2024)

drop if missing(occa1)
collapse (sum) ppopwgt, by(dname occa1 cname year)
    bysort dname: egen total = total(ppopwgt)
    gen percent = ppopwgt / total * 100

decode occa1, gen(occa1_label)
    qui gen code        = real(regexs(1)) if regexm(occa1_label, "\[([^\]]+)\]")
    qui gen short_label = strtrim(substr(occa1_label, strpos(occa1_label, "]") + 1, .))

    // One graph per country, then combine

levelsof cname, local(countries)
local graphs ""
local i 1
foreach country of local countries {
    qui levelsof code if cname == "`country'", local(codes)
    local twoway_cmd ""
    local labels ""
    local j 1 
    foreach c of local codes {
        qui levelsof short_label if code == `c' & cname == "`country'", local(lbl) clean
        local twoway_cmd `"`twoway_cmd' (connected percent year if code == `c' & cname == "`country'", msize(small) lwidth(medthick))"'
        local labels `"`labels' lab(`j' "`lbl'")"'
        local j = `j' + 1
    }
    twoway `twoway_cmd', ///
        ytitle("") xtitle("") ///
        ylabel(0(10)100, angle(horizontal) labsize(vsmall) format(%5.1f)) ///
        xlabel(, labsize(vsmall)) ///
        title("`country'", size(small) color(black)) ///
        graphr(color(white)) plotregion(color(white)) ///
        legend(pos(6) row(2) size(vsmall) `labels') ///
        name(g_`i', replace)
    local graphs "`graphs' g_`i'"
    local i = `i' + 1
}

    // Combine side by side

graph combine `graphs', ///
    cols(2) ///
    graphr(color(white)) ///
    title("Employment by Occupation Group", size(small) color(black)) ///
    caption("LIS - Luxembourg Income Study", size(tiny) position(5))

graph export "$mypdf/ex3.png", replace width(871) height(522)




The previous examples all used standardized LIS variables. This template instead uses region_c, a country-specific variable that is not harmonized across time and countries.
The code manually selects a subset of regions per country using strpos on the decoded label. This is intentional: region_c often contains many categories, and selecting a meaningful subset makes the chart readable. The specific regions chosen here are illustrative.






Note



Manual dataset loop: Unlike the previous examples, which use lissyuse with iso2() to load multiple countries at once, this template loops manually over ccyy codes. This is necessary here because the country-specific filtering on region_c must be applied per dataset before appending results, but it is also a valid general pattern that users can adopt in any of the earlier examples.



clear
tempfile final
save `final', replace emptyok
    
    // Country-specific variables require working with one dataset at a time. 

foreach ccyy in de00 de01 de02 de03 de04 de05 de06 de07 de08 de09 de10 ///
                de11 de12 de13 de14 de15 de16 de17 de18 de19 de20 de21 de22  ///
                it00  it02  it04  it06  it08  it10 ///
                it12  it14  it16    it20  it22   {

    lissyuse, cc(`ccyy') hvars(hid cname year dname dhi nhhmem hwgt region_c)
    qui merge m:1 cname year  using "$myincl/ppp_2021.dta" ,  keep(match)
    drop if missing(dhi)
    generate double new_wgt = nhhmem * hwgt
    
      *--- IQR capping per dataset ---*
    generate double dhi_log = log(dhi)
    replace dhi_log = 0 if dhi_log == . & dhi != .
    sort dhi_log hwgt
    qui percentils dhi_log [aw = hwgt], p(25 75)
    local p75 = e(Perc_75)
    local p25 = e(Perc_25)
    gen double iqr         = `p75' - `p25'
    gen double upper_bound = `p75' + (iqr * 3)
    gen double lower_bound = `p25' - (iqr * 3)
    replace dhi = exp(upper_bound) if dhi > exp(upper_bound)
    replace dhi = exp(lower_bound) if dhi < exp(lower_bound)
    *--- Equivalisation ---*
    replace dhi = dhi / (nhhmem^0.5)
    *--- PPP adjustment ---*
    replace dhi = dhi / lisppp
    *--- Weighted mean by region ---*
    collapse (mean) dhi [aw = new_wgt], by(cname year dname region_c)
 
    
    *--- Decode region and filter selected regions ---*
    decode region_c, gen(region_label)
    keep if strpos(region_label, "Lazio")      | ///
            strpos(region_label, "Lombardia")  | ///
            strpos(region_label, "Campania")   | ///
            strpos(region_label, "Sicilia")    | ///
            strpos(region_label, "Bavaria")    | ///
            strpos(region_label, "Westphalia") | ///
            strpos(region_label, "Baden")      | ///
            strpos(region_label, "Mecklenburg")
    
    append using `final'
    save `final', replace
}
use `final', clear

    // Build twoway dynamically, for each country

qui levelsof cname, local(countries)
local graphs ""
local g = 1
foreach country of local countries {
    qui levelsof region_label if cname == "`country'", local(regions)
    local twoway_cmd ""
    local labels ""
    local i 1
    foreach r of local regions {
        local twoway_cmd `"`twoway_cmd' (connected dhi year if region_label == "`r'" & cname == "`country'", msize(small) lwidth(medthick))"'
        local labels `"`labels' lab(`i' "`r'")"'
        local i = `i' + 1
    }
    twoway `twoway_cmd', ///
        ytitle("") xtitle("") ///
        ylabel(15000(5000)50000, angle(horizontal) labsize(vsmall) format(%8.0gc)) ///
        xlabel(, labsize(vsmall)) ///
        title("`country'", size(small) color(black)) ///
        graphr(color(white)) plotregion(color(white)) ///
        legend(pos(6) col(4) size(tiny) `labels') ///
        name(graph`g', replace)
    local graphs "`graphs' graph`g'"
    local g = `g' + 1
}

    // Combine side by side

graph combine `graphs', ///
    cols(2) ///
    graphr(color(white)) ///
    title("Mean Equivalised Disposable Income by Region", size(small) color(black)) ///
    subtitle("Germany and Italy, selected regions (CPI-adjusted, PPP)", size(vsmall) color(gs8)) ///
    caption("LIS - Luxembourg Income Study", size(tiny) position(5))

graph export "$mypdf/ex4.png", replace width(871) height(522)




This template returns to a standardized LIS variable, and uses it to disaggregate median labour income (pi11) for working-age employed individuals in Sweden and Germany. Unlike the previous examples, which used collapse or percentils inside a loop, this template uses statsby to compute percentiles across all country-sex combinations in a single pass, producing a clean collapsed dataset ready for plotting.
The countries are displayed as facets using by(cname) within twoway, which is a simpler alternative to the graph combine approach when the same set of series (here, male and female) applies to all subplots and a shared legend is desirable.

lissyuse, iso2(se de) pvars(age sex pi11 emp ppopwgt dname cname currency year) from(2002)

drop if ppopwgt == 0 // Such particular cases can be found in DE data for some years (person-level only). 
keep if age > 24 & age < 56 
keep if emp == 1 
keep if !missing(pi11) & !missing(sex)  

    // Deflators
merge m:1 cname year  using "$myincl/ppp_2017.dta" ,  keep(match)      
replace  pi11 =  pi11 / lisppp 

    // Alternative to `collapse` 
statsby ///
    p_50 = e(Perc_50), ///
    by(year cname sex) clear:   ///
    percentils pi11 [aw = ppopwgt], p(50) nose  
    
twoway  (connected p_50 year if sex == 1 ,  msize(small)) ///
        (connected p_50 year if sex == 2,  msize(small)) ///
         , by(cname, legend(pos(6)) note("") graphr(color(white)) caption("Wages expressed in US$ 2017 PPP", size(tiny) position(5)))   leg(col(2) size(vsmall) lab(1 "Male") lab(2 "Female")) ///
          ytitle("Median Wage", size(vsmall)) xtitle("")  ylabel(,  angle(horizontal) labsize(vsmall) format(%8.0fc))  xlabel(2002(6)2020 ,labsize(vsmall)) subtitle(, bcolor(white)  lcolor(white))
                                                    
graph export "$mypdf/ex5.png", replace width(871) height(522)








Tip



statsby for multi-percentile estimation: Unlike collapse, which aggregates data using its own built-in methods, statsby collapses the dataset by subgroups using the stored results of any estimation command. Here it calls percentils once per country-year group and retrieves the stored percentile values directly, allowing multiple percentiles to be computed in a single pass. The nose option suppresses standard errors.




The final template plots multiple derived indicators on the same axes, and extends this to more than one country by wrapping the entire computation in a loop over country codes. Using the United Kingdom and Germany as examples, it computes three percentile ratios (90/10, 90/50, 50/10) of equivalised disposable income and plots them as a time series for each country in separate images.
The key step is reshape long, which converts the three ratio variables into a single ratio variable with a string identifier, making it straightforward to loop over indicators in twoway. This pattern generalises to any situation where multiple computed statistics need to appear on the same plot.






Important



Dynamic export naming: Because this template produces one chart per country within the same job submission, each graph export call must use a unique filename. Here this is achieved by embedding the country code x directly in the filename: ex6_x.png. Without this, each iteration would overwrite the previous file and only the last country’s chart would be retrievable from LISSY output.



local cts uk de 

foreach x of local cts {

lissyuse, iso2(`x') hvars(dhi hwgt nhhmem nhhmem13 cname year dname) from(1970)

levelsof cname, local(levels) 
local ctitle : word 1 of `levels'

drop if missing(dhi) 
drop if missing(nhhmem13) | missing(nhhmem)
replace dhi = dhi / (nhhmem^0.5)

statsby ///
    p_10 = e(Perc_10) ///
    p_50 = e(Perc_50) ///
    p_90 = e(Perc_90), ///
    by(year cname) clear:   ///
    percentils dhi [aw = hwgt], p(10 50 90) nose
        
gen ratio90_10 = p_90 / p_10
gen ratio90_50 = p_90 / p_50
gen ratio50_10 = p_50 / p_10
drop p_*    

reshape long ratio, i(cname year) j(indicator) string

twoway (connected ratio year if indicator == "90_10", msize(small)) ///
       (connected ratio year if indicator == "90_50", msize(small))  ///
       (connected ratio year if indicator == "50_10", msize(small)), ///
       graphr(color(white)) ///
       xlabel(, labsize(vsmall)) ///
       ylabel(0(0.5)5, angle(horizontal) labsize(vsmall)) /// 
       subtitle(, bcolor(white) lcolor(white)) ///
       title("`ctitle' — Inequality Ratios", size(medsmall)) ///
       ytitle("Ratio", size(vsmall)) xtitle("") ///
       leg(col(3) pos(6) size(vsmall) lab(1 "90/10") lab(2 "90/50") lab(3 "50/10")) 

graph export `"$mypdf/ex6_`x'.png"', replace width(871) height(522)       
       
}

    foreach c of local codes {
        qui levelsof short_label if code == `c' & cname == "`country'", local(lbl) clean
        local twoway_cmd `"`twoway_cmd' (connected percent year if code == `c' & cname == "`country'", msize(small) lwidth(medthick))"'
        local labels `"`labels' lab(`j' "`lbl'")"'
        local j = `j' + 1
    }
    twoway `twoway_cmd', ///
        ytitle("") xtitle("") ///
        ylabel(0(10)100, angle(horizontal) labsize(vsmall) format(%5.1f)) ///
        xlabel(, labsize(vsmall)) ///
        title("`country'", size(small) color(black)) ///
        graphr(color(white)) plotregion(color(white)) ///
        legend(pos(6) row(2) size(vsmall) `labels') ///
        name(g_`i', replace)
    local graphs "`graphs' g_`i'"
    local i = `i' + 1
}

    // Combine side by side

graph combine `graphs', ///
    cols(2) ///
    graphr(color(white)) ///
    title("Employment by Occupation Group", size(small) color(black)) ///
    caption("LIS - Luxembourg Income Study", size(tiny) position(5))

graph export "$mypdf/ex3.png", replace width(871) height(522)

title: Structuring Results for Analysis
text:
The previous examples all used standardized LIS variables. This template instead uses region_c, a country-specific variable that is not harmonized across time and countries.
The code manually selects a subset of regions per country using strpos on the decoded label. This is intentional: region_c often contains many categories, and selecting a meaningful subset makes the chart readable. The specific regions chosen here are illustrative.






Note



Manual dataset loop: Unlike the previous examples, which use lissyuse with iso2() to load multiple countries at once, this template loops manually over ccyy codes. This is necessary here because the country-specific filtering on region_c must be applied per dataset before appending results, but it is also a valid general pattern that users can adopt in any of the earlier examples.



clear
tempfile final
save `final', replace emptyok
    
    // Country-specific variables require working with one dataset at a time. 

foreach ccyy in de00 de01 de02 de03 de04 de05 de06 de07 de08 de09 de10 ///
                de11 de12 de13 de14 de15 de16 de17 de18 de19 de20 de21 de22  ///
                it00  it02  it04  it06  it08  it10 ///
                it12  it14  it16    it20  it22   {

    lissyuse, cc(`ccyy') hvars(hid cname year dname dhi nhhmem hwgt region_c)
    qui merge m:1 cname year  using "$myincl/ppp_2021.dta" ,  keep(match)
    drop if missing(dhi)
    generate double new_wgt = nhhmem * hwgt
    
      *--- IQR capping per dataset ---*
    generate double dhi_log = log(dhi)
    replace dhi_log = 0 if dhi_log == . & dhi != .
    sort dhi_log hwgt
    qui percentils dhi_log [aw = hwgt], p(25 75)
    local p75 = e(Perc_75)
    local p25 = e(Perc_25)
    gen double iqr         = `p75' - `p25'
    gen double upper_bound = `p75' + (iqr * 3)
    gen double lower_bound = `p25' - (iqr * 3)
    replace dhi = exp(upper_bound) if dhi > exp(upper_bound)
    replace dhi = exp(lower_bound) if dhi < exp(lower_bound)
    *--- Equivalisation ---*
    replace dhi = dhi / (nhhmem^0.5)
    *--- PPP adjustment ---*
    replace dhi = dhi / lisppp
    *--- Weighted mean by region ---*
    collapse (mean) dhi [aw = new_wgt], by(cname year dname region_c)
 
    
    *--- Decode region and filter selected regions ---*
    decode region_c, gen(region_label)
    keep if strpos(region_label, "Lazio")      | ///
            strpos(region_label, "Lombardia")  | ///
            strpos(region_label, "Campania")   | ///
            strpos(region_label, "Sicilia")    | ///
            strpos(region_label, "Bavaria")    | ///
            strpos(region_label, "Westphalia") | ///
            strpos(region_label, "Baden")      | ///
            strpos(region_label, "Mecklenburg")
    
    append using `final'
    save `final', replace
}
use `final', clear

    // Build twoway dynamically, for each country

qui levelsof cname, local(countries)
local graphs ""
local g = 1
foreach country of local countries {
    qui levelsof region_label if cname == "`country'", local(regions)
    local twoway_cmd ""
    local labels ""
    local i 1
    foreach r of local regions {
        local twoway_cmd `"`twoway_cmd' (connected dhi year if region_label == "`r'" & cname == "`country'", msize(small) lwidth(medthick))"'
        local labels `"`labels' lab(`i' "`r'")"'
        local i = `i' + 1
    }
    twoway `twoway_cmd', ///
        ytitle("") xtitle("") ///
        ylabel(15000(5000)50000, angle(horizontal) labsize(vsmall) format(%8.0gc)) ///
        xlabel(, labsize(vsmall)) ///
        title("`country'", size(small) color(black)) ///
        graphr(color(white)) plotregion(color(white)) ///
        legend(pos(6) col(4) size(tiny) `labels') ///
        name(graph`g', replace)
    local graphs "`graphs' graph`g'"
    local g = `g' + 1
}

    // Combine side by side

graph combine `graphs', ///
    cols(2) ///
    graphr(color(white)) ///
    title("Mean Equivalised Disposable Income by Region", size(small) color(black)) ///
    subtitle("Germany and Italy, selected regions (CPI-adjusted, PPP)", size(vsmall) color(gs8)) ///
    caption("LIS - Luxembourg Income Study", size(tiny) position(5))

graph export "$mypdf/ex4.png", replace width(871) height(522)

title: Structuring Results for Analysis
text:
This template returns to a standardized LIS variable, and uses it to disaggregate median labour income (pi11) for working-age employed individuals in Sweden and Germany. Unlike the previous examples, which used collapse or percentils inside a loop, this template uses statsby to compute percentiles across all country-sex combinations in a single pass, producing a clean collapsed dataset ready for plotting.
The countries are displayed as facets using by(cname) within twoway, which is a simpler alternative to the graph combine approach when the same set of series (here, male and female) applies to all subplots and a shared legend is desirable.

lissyuse, iso2(se de) pvars(age sex pi11 emp ppopwgt dname cname currency year) from(2002)

drop if ppopwgt == 0 // Such particular cases can be found in DE data for some years (person-level only). 
keep if age > 24 & age < 56 
keep if emp == 1 
keep if !missing(pi11) & !missing(sex)  

    // Deflators
merge m:1 cname year  using "$myincl/ppp_2017.dta" ,  keep(match)      
replace  pi11 =  pi11 / lisppp 

    // Alternative to `collapse` 
statsby ///
    p_50 = e(Perc_50), ///
    by(year cname sex) clear:   ///
    percentils pi11 [aw = ppopwgt], p(50) nose  
    
twoway  (connected p_50 year if sex == 1 ,  msize(small)) ///
        (connected p_50 year if sex == 2,  msize(small)) ///
         , by(cname, legend(pos(6)) note("") graphr(color(white)) caption("Wages expressed in US$ 2017 PPP", size(tiny) position(5)))   leg(col(2) size(vsmall) lab(1 "Male") lab(2 "Female")) ///
          ytitle("Median Wage", size(vsmall)) xtitle("")  ylabel(,  angle(horizontal) labsize(vsmall) format(%8.0fc))  xlabel(2002(6)2020 ,labsize(vsmall)) subtitle(, bcolor(white)  lcolor(white))
                                                    
graph export "$mypdf/ex5.png", replace width(871) height(522)








Tip



statsby for multi-percentile estimation: Unlike collapse, which aggregates data using its own built-in methods, statsby collapses the dataset by subgroups using the stored results of any estimation command. Here it calls percentils once per country-year group and retrieves the stored percentile values directly, allowing multiple percentiles to be computed in a single pass. The nose option suppresses standard errors.

title: Structuring Results for Analysis
text:
The final template plots multiple derived indicators on the same axes, and extends this to more than one country by wrapping the entire computation in a loop over country codes. Using the United Kingdom and Germany as examples, it computes three percentile ratios (90/10, 90/50, 50/10) of equivalised disposable income and plots them as a time series for each country in separate images.
The key step is reshape long, which converts the three ratio variables into a single ratio variable with a string identifier, making it straightforward to loop over indicators in twoway. This pattern generalises to any situation where multiple computed statistics need to appear on the same plot.






Important



Dynamic export naming: Because this template produces one chart per country within the same job submission, each graph export call must use a unique filename. Here this is achieved by embedding the country code x directly in the filename: ex6_x.png. Without this, each iteration would overwrite the previous file and only the last country’s chart would be retrievable from LISSY output.



local cts uk de 

foreach x of local cts {

lissyuse, iso2(`x') hvars(dhi hwgt nhhmem nhhmem13 cname year dname) from(1970)

levelsof cname, local(levels) 
local ctitle : word 1 of `levels'

drop if missing(dhi) 
drop if missing(nhhmem13) | missing(nhhmem)
replace dhi = dhi / (nhhmem^0.5)

statsby ///
    p_10 = e(Perc_10) ///
    p_50 = e(Perc_50) ///
    p_90 = e(Perc_90), ///
    by(year cname) clear:   ///
    percentils dhi [aw = hwgt], p(10 50 90) nose
        
gen ratio90_10 = p_90 / p_10
gen ratio90_50 = p_90 / p_50
gen ratio50_10 = p_50 / p_10
drop p_*    

reshape long ratio, i(cname year) j(indicator) string

twoway (connected ratio year if indicator == "90_10", msize(small)) ///
       (connected ratio year if indicator == "90_50", msize(small))  ///
       (connected ratio year if indicator == "50_10", msize(small)), ///
       graphr(color(white)) ///
       xlabel(, labsize(vsmall)) ///
       ylabel(0(0.5)5, angle(horizontal) labsize(vsmall)) /// 
       subtitle(, bcolor(white) lcolor(white)) ///
       title("`ctitle' — Inequality Ratios", size(medsmall)) ///
       ytitle("Ratio", size(vsmall)) xtitle("") ///
       leg(col(3) pos(6) size(vsmall) lab(1 "90/10") lab(2 "90/50") lab(3 "50/10")) 

graph export `"$mypdf/ex6_`x'.png"', replace width(871) height(522)       
       
}

title: Import Data
text:
Method 2 - use command.
As with any other .dta file stored locally in Stata, LIS microdata files can also be accessed directly using Stata’s native use command.
The main drawback of this approach is that the user must manually manage the entire import process. This includes:

specifying each ccyy dataset individually
identifying the correct available years
importing household-level (h) and person-level (p) files separately
merging both data levels manually
appending all datasets together
managing temporary files throughout the workflow

The example below illustrates a typical workflow using Stata’s native commands. For each country–year dataset, the person-level file is first loaded, household-level variables are then merged using the household identifier (hid), and the resulting datasets are progressively appended into a single combined file.

global varshh "hid own"
* Person-level variables
global varspp "hid dname pwgt ppopwgt relation partner ageyoch age sex immigr educ emp status1 ptime1 hwage1"
* Country-year datasets
global datasets "us04 be04 gr04"
* Temporary file to store appended results
tempfile master
save `master', emptyok replace
foreach ccyy in $datasets {
    * Load person-level file
    use $varspp using $`ccyy'p, clear
    * Merge household-level variables
    merge m:1 hid using $`ccyy'h, ///
        keepusing($varshh) nogen
    * Append to master dataset
    append using `master'
    * Save updated combined dataset
    save `master', replace
}
* Load final combined dataset
use `master', clear
tab dname 
* Example summary statistics
tabstat sex, by(dname)
tabstat own, by(dname)

Although this method remains fully valid and may provide more granular control for advanced users, lissyuse considerably simplifies the workflow by automating dataset selection, merging, appending, and data-level management procedures.






Tip



When loading LIS datasets with Stata’s use command, always prefix the dataset name with $ and specify the corresponding data level suffix: h for household-level files and p for person-level files.

title: Data Handling
text:
Due to the wide range of research questions that can be explored using data from LIS, it is often necessary to perform multiple and distinct types of data preparation after the initial import. For this reason, this section is divided into two parts, each dedicated to a different analytical goal.
In the first part, we demonstrate how to compute a Children Poverty Rate among Single-Mother Families. This particular indicator requires several steps, making it a comprehensive example of the types of Stata functions users can rely on, as well as highlighting important considerations when working with LIS/LWS/LCS data.
In the second part, we focus on how to apply the deflators provided by LIS, an essential step for cross-country and cross-time comparisons, and discuss the specific nuances involved in that process.


The sections that follow illustrate a more comprehensive workflow, combining several preparation steps to construct a policy-relevant indicator from microdata.
The aim will be to compute the poverty rate among children in single-mother households in several countries. Constructing this indicator requires combining information available at both the household level (dhi, nhhmem17, hpartner), and the individual level (sex).






Important



Recall from the earlier sections of this guidebook when we introduced the lissyuse command, that when both household and individual variables are specified, both files for a given ccyy are loaded and merged automatically. As a result, the data loaded is at the individual-level.



qui lissyuse, iso2(us de uk fr) from(2018) to(2024) hvars(hid cname dname year dhi nhhmem nhhmem17 hpartner hwgt) pvars(pid sex relation)



At this stage, we prepare the dataset so that it is aligned with the unit of analysis required for our indicator: the household. Although we imported both household- and person-level variables, the poverty measure is computed at the household level and then attributed to individuals (in this case, children).
Since in the importing stage we retrieve microdata for several waves appended into a single dataset, the transformations described below must be applied to each ccyy separately. At the end of this section we present the complete routine, which uses a loop together with the preserve/restore technique. For now, we walk through each transformation step individually.

*===================================
* Keep only household heads
*===================================    

drop if relation != 1000 // (data is now at household-level)    

*===================================
* Filter out missing observations 
*===================================
     
drop if missing(dhi)
     
*===================================
* Create person\children weights (data is at household-level)
*===================================
     
generate double pwt = hwgt * nhhmem 
generate double cwt = hwgt * nhhmem17 

We begin by retaining only records corresponding to the household reference person (relation == 1000). This step ensures that each household appears exactly once in the dataset, avoiding the duplication that would arise from keeping all person-level records. We then drop observations with missing disposable household income (dhi), as these cannot contribute to the poverty calculation.
Next, we construct two adjusted weights. For population-level indicators, we use a person-level weight derived from the household weight multiplied by household size (hwgt * nhhmem). For child-specific indicators, we construct a child weight by multiplying the household weight by the number of children in the household (hwgt * nhhmem17). These weights ensure that estimates correctly reflect the underlying population structure.


Before proceeding with inequality and poverty calculations, we address the presence of extreme income values. While the underlying microdata do not impose bounds on income, very high or very low values can disproportionately influence distributional measures.
To mitigate this, we apply bottom- and top-coding to disposable household income (dhi). For methodological consistency with the rest of the workflow, we use the percentils command introduced in the previous sections to estimate the relevant percentiles.


*===================================
* Bottom and top coding / outlier detection
*===================================

generate double dhi_log = log(dhi) 
replace dhi_log = 0 if dhi_log == . & dhi != .        // keep negatives and 0 

sort dhi_log hwgt
qui percentils dhi_log [aw = hwgt], p(25 75)
local p75 = e(Perc_75)
local p25 = e(Perc_25) 
gen double iqr = `p75' - `p25'                        // interquartile range
gen double upper_bound = `p75'  + (iqr * 3)           // upper bound for extreme values
gen double lower_bound = `p25'  - (iqr * 3)           // lower bound for extreme values
replace dhi=exp(upper_bound) if dhi>exp(upper_bound)  // top code income at upper bound for extreme values
replace dhi=exp(lower_bound) if dhi<exp(lower_bound)  // bottom code income at lower bound for extreme values







Note



The sort step helps maintain consistency when assessing the position of observations that share the same income value. Using double precision throughout helps preserve numerical accuracy and avoids rounding errors that can accumulate in distributional calculations.


This adjustment is carried out on the logarithmic scale. An interquartile range (IQR) rule is applied: values above the upper threshold (Q3 + 3×IQR) are capped, and values below the lower threshold (Q1 − 3×IQR) are raised. Working on the log scale has the advantage of making the IQR rule less sensitive to the heavy right-skew that is typical of income distributions. The back-transformation via exp() then brings the bounds back to the original income scale. This approach ensures that extreme observations do not disproportionately affect results, while preserving the overall shape and structure of the income distribution.






Note



To ensure consistency with the methodology applied by LIS across all disseminated aggregate figures, this step must be performed prior to equivalisation. In addition, the quartiles used to define the IQR thresholds should be estimated following Definition 4 as proposed by Hyndman and Fan (1996).




Households differ in size and composition, which affects their economic needs. To enable meaningful comparisons across households, we equivalize disposable household income.
We apply the square root equivalence scale, dividing household income by the square root of the total number of household members. This transformation accounts for economies of scale in consumption: larger households require more resources, but not proportionally more per additional member.
As a result, all individuals within a household are assigned the same equivalised income, regardless of their age or role within the household.

*===================================
* Equivalise income (square root)
*===================================
generate double ey = ( dhi / (nhhmem^0.5) )



Having adjusted the income variable and reduced the dataset to the household level, we are now ready to compute the poverty line. We define it as 50% of the weighted median of equivalised income,
Because percentils stores results in scalars using the naming convention e(Perc_XX), the median can be retrieved directly as e(Perc_50) and then halved to obtain the threshold. Note that the median is estimated on the ey variable using the person-level weight pwt, which ensures it represents the distribution across individuals rather than households.

*===================================
* Compute Poverty Line
*===================================
sort ey pwt 
qui percentils ey [aw= pwt], p(50) // median    
qui gen double poverty_line_50  = e(Perc_50) * 0.5

It is important to note that the poverty line is always calculated based on the full population. This same threshold is then applied when evaluating poverty rates for specific subgroups, such as children in single-mother households.


In the final step, we restrict the sample to the population of interest: children living in single-mother households. This is defined as households where the reference person is female (sex == 2), has no partner present (hpartner == 0), and where at least one child is present (nhhmem17 > 0).
We first generate the binary poverty indicator, then compute its weighted mean using the child-specific weight (cwt). This produces the poverty rate among children in single-mother households, expressed as a percentage.

*===================================
* Children Poverty Rates - Single Mother Family (50%)
*===================================    
qui sum pov50 [w=cwt] if hpartner == 0 & /// 
                              sex == 2 & ///
                              nhhmem17 > 0
                             
display "Children Poverty Rates - Single-Mother Families (50%) = " r(mean) 



The code below extends the single-country workflow to multiple countries and waves. It follows the same logical steps as before, but wraps them in a loop that iterates over each dataset (ccyy) identified in the pooled data loaded by lissyuse.

    // 1) Load data 

qui lissyuse, iso2(us de uk fr) ///
              from(2018) to(2024) /// 
              hvars(hid cname dname year dhi nhhmem nhhmem17 hpartner hwgt) /// 
              pvars(pid sex relation) // (data is at person-level)

*==========================================
* Identify and loop over selected datasets
*=========================================

levelsof dname, local(levels)
foreach ccyy of local levels {
        
    **
    preserve
    **
    qui {
    keep if dname == "`ccyy'"


        // 2) Data preparation 

    *===================================
    * Keep only household heads
    *===================================    

    drop if relation != 1000 // (data is at household-level)    

    *===================================
    * Filter out missing observations 
    *===================================
     
    drop if missing(dhi)
     
    *===================================
    * Create person\children\elderly weights (data is at household-level)
    *===================================
     
    generate double pwt = hwgt * nhhmem 
    generate double cwt = hwgt * nhhmem17 
     
    *===================================
    * Bottom and top coding / outlier detection
    *===================================

    generate double dhi_log = log(dhi) 
    replace dhi_log = 0 if dhi_log == . & dhi != . // keep negatives and 0 

    sort dhi_log hwgt
    qui percentils dhi_log [aw = hwgt], p(25 75)
    local p75 = e(Perc_75)
    local p25 = e(Perc_25) 
    gen double iqr = `p75' - `p25'  // interquartile range
    gen double upper_bound = `p75'  + (iqr * 3)  // upper bound for extreme values
    gen double lower_bound = `p25'  - (iqr * 3)  // lower bound for extreme values
    replace dhi=exp(upper_bound) if dhi>exp(upper_bound)  // top code income at upper bound for extreme values
    replace dhi=exp(lower_bound) if dhi<exp(lower_bound)  // bottom code income at lower bound for extreme values

    *===================================
    * Equivalise income (square root)
    *===================================
    generate double ey = ( dhi / (nhhmem^0.5) )


        // 3) Compute Key Figures 
        
    sort ey pwt 
    qui percentils ey [aw= pwt], p(50) // median    
    qui gen double poverty_line_50  = e(Perc_50) * 0.5


    qui gen double pov50 = 0 if !missing(ey)
    replace pov50 = 100 if ey < poverty_line_50 

    *===================================
    * Children Poverty Rates - Single Mother Family (50%)
    *===================================    
    qui sum pov50 [w=cwt] if hpartner == 0 & /// 
                             sex == 2 & ///
                             nhhmem17 > 0
    }                        
    display "`ccyy'" "," "Children Poverty Rates - Single-Mother Families (50%)" "," r(mean)    
        
    **
    restore
    **

}

Several features of this routine are worth noting.

levelsof and the loop. After loading the pooled dataset, levelsof dname extracts the full list of unique dataset identifiers — one per country-wave combination (e.g., us19, de20) — and stores them in the local macro levels. The foreach loop then iterates over this list, processing each dataset in turn. This avoids hardcoding country-year combinations and makes the routine straightforward to extend to additional countries or time periods simply by adjusting the arguments passed to lissyuse.
preserve and restore. Because all waves and countries are held in memory simultaneously as a single pooled dataset, any modification made inside the loop — such as dropping observations or generating new variables — would otherwise permanently alter the data for all subsequent iterations. The preserve command saves a snapshot of the full dataset in memory at the start of each iteration, and restore reinstates it at the end, ensuring that each pass through the loop starts from the same complete pooled dataset.
Comma-separated output. The display statement at the end of each iteration prints the dataset identifier, the indicator label, and the estimated poverty rate as a comma-separated line. This format is deliberately chosen for its portability: the output can be copied directly into a spreadsheet or text file and parsed without any further reformatting.

qui lissyuse, iso2(us de uk fr) from(2018) to(2024) hvars(hid cname dname year dhi nhhmem nhhmem17 hpartner hwgt) pvars(pid sex relation)

title: Data Handling
text:
At this stage, we prepare the dataset so that it is aligned with the unit of analysis required for our indicator: the household. Although we imported both household- and person-level variables, the poverty measure is computed at the household level and then attributed to individuals (in this case, children).
Since in the importing stage we retrieve microdata for several waves appended into a single dataset, the transformations described below must be applied to each ccyy separately. At the end of this section we present the complete routine, which uses a loop together with the preserve/restore technique. For now, we walk through each transformation step individually.

*===================================
* Keep only household heads
*===================================    

drop if relation != 1000 // (data is now at household-level)    

*===================================
* Filter out missing observations 
*===================================
     
drop if missing(dhi)
     
*===================================
* Create person\children weights (data is at household-level)
*===================================
     
generate double pwt = hwgt * nhhmem 
generate double cwt = hwgt * nhhmem17 

We begin by retaining only records corresponding to the household reference person (relation == 1000). This step ensures that each household appears exactly once in the dataset, avoiding the duplication that would arise from keeping all person-level records. We then drop observations with missing disposable household income (dhi), as these cannot contribute to the poverty calculation.
Next, we construct two adjusted weights. For population-level indicators, we use a person-level weight derived from the household weight multiplied by household size (hwgt * nhhmem). For child-specific indicators, we construct a child weight by multiplying the household weight by the number of children in the household (hwgt * nhhmem17). These weights ensure that estimates correctly reflect the underlying population structure.

title: Data Handling
text:
Before proceeding with inequality and poverty calculations, we address the presence of extreme income values. While the underlying microdata do not impose bounds on income, very high or very low values can disproportionately influence distributional measures.
To mitigate this, we apply bottom- and top-coding to disposable household income (dhi). For methodological consistency with the rest of the workflow, we use the percentils command introduced in the previous sections to estimate the relevant percentiles.


*===================================
* Bottom and top coding / outlier detection
*===================================

generate double dhi_log = log(dhi) 
replace dhi_log = 0 if dhi_log == . & dhi != .        // keep negatives and 0 

sort dhi_log hwgt
qui percentils dhi_log [aw = hwgt], p(25 75)
local p75 = e(Perc_75)
local p25 = e(Perc_25) 
gen double iqr = `p75' - `p25'                        // interquartile range
gen double upper_bound = `p75'  + (iqr * 3)           // upper bound for extreme values
gen double lower_bound = `p25'  - (iqr * 3)           // lower bound for extreme values
replace dhi=exp(upper_bound) if dhi>exp(upper_bound)  // top code income at upper bound for extreme values
replace dhi=exp(lower_bound) if dhi<exp(lower_bound)  // bottom code income at lower bound for extreme values







Note



The sort step helps maintain consistency when assessing the position of observations that share the same income value. Using double precision throughout helps preserve numerical accuracy and avoids rounding errors that can accumulate in distributional calculations.


This adjustment is carried out on the logarithmic scale. An interquartile range (IQR) rule is applied: values above the upper threshold (Q3 + 3×IQR) are capped, and values below the lower threshold (Q1 − 3×IQR) are raised. Working on the log scale has the advantage of making the IQR rule less sensitive to the heavy right-skew that is typical of income distributions. The back-transformation via exp() then brings the bounds back to the original income scale. This approach ensures that extreme observations do not disproportionately affect results, while preserving the overall shape and structure of the income distribution.






Note



To ensure consistency with the methodology applied by LIS across all disseminated aggregate figures, this step must be performed prior to equivalisation. In addition, the quartiles used to define the IQR thresholds should be estimated following Definition 4 as proposed by Hyndman and Fan (1996).

title: Data Handling
text:
Households differ in size and composition, which affects their economic needs. To enable meaningful comparisons across households, we equivalize disposable household income.
We apply the square root equivalence scale, dividing household income by the square root of the total number of household members. This transformation accounts for economies of scale in consumption: larger households require more resources, but not proportionally more per additional member.
As a result, all individuals within a household are assigned the same equivalised income, regardless of their age or role within the household.

*===================================
* Equivalise income (square root)
*===================================
generate double ey = ( dhi / (nhhmem^0.5) )

title: Data Handling
text:
Having adjusted the income variable and reduced the dataset to the household level, we are now ready to compute the poverty line. We define it as 50% of the weighted median of equivalised income,
Because percentils stores results in scalars using the naming convention e(Perc_XX), the median can be retrieved directly as e(Perc_50) and then halved to obtain the threshold. Note that the median is estimated on the ey variable using the person-level weight pwt, which ensures it represents the distribution across individuals rather than households.

*===================================
* Compute Poverty Line
*===================================
sort ey pwt 
qui percentils ey [aw= pwt], p(50) // median    
qui gen double poverty_line_50  = e(Perc_50) * 0.5

It is important to note that the poverty line is always calculated based on the full population. This same threshold is then applied when evaluating poverty rates for specific subgroups, such as children in single-mother households.

title: Data Handling
text:
In the final step, we restrict the sample to the population of interest: children living in single-mother households. This is defined as households where the reference person is female (sex == 2), has no partner present (hpartner == 0), and where at least one child is present (nhhmem17 > 0).
We first generate the binary poverty indicator, then compute its weighted mean using the child-specific weight (cwt). This produces the poverty rate among children in single-mother households, expressed as a percentage.

*===================================
* Children Poverty Rates - Single Mother Family (50%)
*===================================    
qui sum pov50 [w=cwt] if hpartner == 0 & /// 
                              sex == 2 & ///
                              nhhmem17 > 0
                             
display "Children Poverty Rates - Single-Mother Families (50%) = " r(mean)

title: Data Handling
text:
The code below extends the single-country workflow to multiple countries and waves. It follows the same logical steps as before, but wraps them in a loop that iterates over each dataset (ccyy) identified in the pooled data loaded by lissyuse.

    // 1) Load data 

qui lissyuse, iso2(us de uk fr) ///
              from(2018) to(2024) /// 
              hvars(hid cname dname year dhi nhhmem nhhmem17 hpartner hwgt) /// 
              pvars(pid sex relation) // (data is at person-level)

*==========================================
* Identify and loop over selected datasets
*=========================================

levelsof dname, local(levels)
foreach ccyy of local levels {
        
    **
    preserve
    **
    qui {
    keep if dname == "`ccyy'"


        // 2) Data preparation 

    *===================================
    * Keep only household heads
    *===================================    

    drop if relation != 1000 // (data is at household-level)    

    *===================================
    * Filter out missing observations 
    *===================================
     
    drop if missing(dhi)
     
    *===================================
    * Create person\children\elderly weights (data is at household-level)
    *===================================
     
    generate double pwt = hwgt * nhhmem 
    generate double cwt = hwgt * nhhmem17 
     
    *===================================
    * Bottom and top coding / outlier detection
    *===================================

    generate double dhi_log = log(dhi) 
    replace dhi_log = 0 if dhi_log == . & dhi != . // keep negatives and 0 

    sort dhi_log hwgt
    qui percentils dhi_log [aw = hwgt], p(25 75)
    local p75 = e(Perc_75)
    local p25 = e(Perc_25) 
    gen double iqr = `p75' - `p25'  // interquartile range
    gen double upper_bound = `p75'  + (iqr * 3)  // upper bound for extreme values
    gen double lower_bound = `p25'  - (iqr * 3)  // lower bound for extreme values
    replace dhi=exp(upper_bound) if dhi>exp(upper_bound)  // top code income at upper bound for extreme values
    replace dhi=exp(lower_bound) if dhi<exp(lower_bound)  // bottom code income at lower bound for extreme values

    *===================================
    * Equivalise income (square root)
    *===================================
    generate double ey = ( dhi / (nhhmem^0.5) )


        // 3) Compute Key Figures 
        
    sort ey pwt 
    qui percentils ey [aw= pwt], p(50) // median    
    qui gen double poverty_line_50  = e(Perc_50) * 0.5


    qui gen double pov50 = 0 if !missing(ey)
    replace pov50 = 100 if ey < poverty_line_50 

    *===================================
    * Children Poverty Rates - Single Mother Family (50%)
    *===================================    
    qui sum pov50 [w=cwt] if hpartner == 0 & /// 
                             sex == 2 & ///
                             nhhmem17 > 0
    }                        
    display "`ccyy'" "," "Children Poverty Rates - Single-Mother Families (50%)" "," r(mean)    
        
    **
    restore
    **

}

Several features of this routine are worth noting.

levelsof and the loop. After loading the pooled dataset, levelsof dname extracts the full list of unique dataset identifiers — one per country-wave combination (e.g., us19, de20) — and stores them in the local macro levels. The foreach loop then iterates over this list, processing each dataset in turn. This avoids hardcoding country-year combinations and makes the routine straightforward to extend to additional countries or time periods simply by adjusting the arguments passed to lissyuse.
preserve and restore. Because all waves and countries are held in memory simultaneously as a single pooled dataset, any modification made inside the loop — such as dropping observations or generating new variables — would otherwise permanently alter the data for all subsequent iterations. The preserve command saves a snapshot of the full dataset in memory at the start of each iteration, and restore reinstates it at the end, ensuring that each pass through the loop starts from the same complete pooled dataset.
Comma-separated output. The display statement at the end of each iteration prints the dataset identifier, the indicator label, and the estimated poverty rate as a comma-separated line. This format is deliberately chosen for its portability: the output can be copied directly into a spreadsheet or text file and parsed without any further reformatting.

title: Describing Data
text:
In LIS/LWS/LCS datasets, continuous variables are distinct from the socioeconomic categorical variables discussed in the previous section. Rather than grouping households or individuals into discrete classes, they capture actual flows and stocks — income, consumption, and wealth, along with their subcomponents and aggregates. Examples include disposable household income (dhi), capital income (hicapital), and net worth (dnw). These variables tend to be right-skewed, can span several orders of magnitude, and vary considerably in coverage across country-years — a variable that is well-populated in one dataset may be sparse or entirely absent in another. Getting a quick distributional snapshot before any substantive analysis is therefore good practice. The emphasis in this section is not so much on the mechanics of any single statistic, but on building reproducible workflows that apply consistently across countries and waves with minimal extra effort.


A natural starting point is to use the summarize command to obtain an initial overview of a variable’s scale and distribution, iterating across datasets via by dname:.






Tip



Always make sure the data is at the appropriate level for the variable being analysed. Disposable household income (dhi), for instance, is defined at the household level. Running summary statistics on it from an individual-level dataset will silently duplicate observations, inflating counts and distorting distributional measures.

Warning



While summarize, detail provides a convenient initial overview, its distributional measures (e.g., the median, p25, and p75) do not follow the methodology used by LIS in its official figures. This is discussed in more detail later in this section.



Beyond summary statistics, it is often useful to compute a specific diagnostic and apply it systematically across all available datasets. This keeps the workflow transparent and easy to replicate.
As a practical illustration, consider measuring data coverage: for a given income component, what share of observations are both non-missing and non-zero? This is especially relevant for variables like capital income (hicapital), which may be consistently recorded in some country-years but sparse or absent in others.

qui lissyuse, iso2(it) from(2005) hvars(hid cname year dname dhi hicapital)

gen byte has_inc   = (!missing(hicapital) & hicapital != 0)   
gen byte obs_count = 1 

egen total_obs    = total(obs_count), by(dname)
egen nonmiss_obs  = total(has_inc)  , by(dname)

gen pct_nonmiss = (nonmiss_obs / total_obs) * 100
bysort dname: keep if _n == 1 // keeping one row per dname (mimics collapse)

keep cname year total_obs nonmiss_obs pct_nonmiss
forvalues i = 1/`=_N' {
   if `i' == 1 {
     di "cname,year,total_obs,nonmiss_obs,pct_nonmiss"
        } 
     di cname[`i'] ","  year[`i'] "," total_obs[`i'] "," nonmiss_obs[`i'] "," pct_nonmiss[`i']
}

Aggregate statistics can conceal important variation across groups. For continuous variables, computing descriptives by subgroup makes it possible to compare, for instance, how disposable income differs across tenure statuses or demographic categories.
As seen in the section on categorical variables, collapse is a natural tool for this in Stata. Here the same logic applies, with (mean) as the descriptive measure of interest, though this can be replaced by any other statistic supported by the command, such as (median), (sd), or (p25) and (p75). The by() option ensures the computation is carried out separately for each combination of dataset and tenure group:


qui lissyuse, iso2(fr it es de) from(2021) hvars(hid dhi hwgt dname cname year own)
collapse (mean) avg_dhi = dhi, by(dname own cname year)
    
    decode own, gen(own_label)
    qui gen code = real(regexs(1)) if regexm(own_label, "\[([^\]]+)\]")
    qui gen label = substr(own_label, strpos(own_label, "]") + 1, .)


forvalues i = 1/`=_N' {
   if `i' == 1 {
     di "cname,year,code,label,avg_dhi"
        } 
     di cname[`i'] "," year[`i'] "," code[`i'] "," label[`i'] "," avg_dhi[`i'] 
}

Note



The two gen lines above handle a recurrent situation in LIS data. The variable own is originally numeric with value labels — category 110 is stored as the number 110 and displayed as owned outright. After decode, it becomes the plain string [110]owned outright. While readable, this single string is harder to filter or sort programmatically. The two lines split it back into its two components: code recovers the numeric part (110) by extracting the content inside the brackets, and label recovers the clean text (owned outright) by taking everything after the closing bracket. This gives you a tidy, analysis-ready output where the category code and its description live in separate variables.




We close with an important note on how percentiles are estimated, as the choice of method directly affects the comparability of results with LIS official figures.
Although percentile-based measures do not introduce fundamentally new techniques beyond those discussed above, it is important to clarify the methodology used by LIS, as this directly affects the comparability and reproducibility of results.
LIS adopts Definition 4 from Hyndman and Fan (1996) for the computation of key figures and all percentile-based estimates, including medians, percentile ratios, poverty lines, and decile shares. The command percentils is a custom command that follows this methodology by default, so users can rely on it to produce estimates fully consistent with LIS standards without needing to configure anything manually.

qui lissyuse, iso2(es it) hvars(hid hpopwgt dhi cname year dname) from(2020)

* `statsby` mimics `collapse` using the stored results from the selected command  

statsby ///
    p_50 = e(Perc_50), ///
    by(year cname) clear:   ///
    percentils dhi [aw = hpopwgt], p(50) nose   
sort cname year

forvalues i = 1/`=_N' {
   if `i' == 1 {
     di "year,cname,p_50"
        } 
     di year[`i'] "," cname[`i'] "," p_50[`i']
}

(running percentils on estimation sample)

title: Describing Data
text:
Beyond summary statistics, it is often useful to compute a specific diagnostic and apply it systematically across all available datasets. This keeps the workflow transparent and easy to replicate.
As a practical illustration, consider measuring data coverage: for a given income component, what share of observations are both non-missing and non-zero? This is especially relevant for variables like capital income (hicapital), which may be consistently recorded in some country-years but sparse or absent in others.

qui lissyuse, iso2(it) from(2005) hvars(hid cname year dname dhi hicapital)

gen byte has_inc   = (!missing(hicapital) & hicapital != 0)   
gen byte obs_count = 1 

egen total_obs    = total(obs_count), by(dname)
egen nonmiss_obs  = total(has_inc)  , by(dname)

gen pct_nonmiss = (nonmiss_obs / total_obs) * 100
bysort dname: keep if _n == 1 // keeping one row per dname (mimics collapse)

keep cname year total_obs nonmiss_obs pct_nonmiss
forvalues i = 1/`=_N' {
   if `i' == 1 {
     di "cname,year,total_obs,nonmiss_obs,pct_nonmiss"
        } 
     di cname[`i'] ","  year[`i'] "," total_obs[`i'] "," nonmiss_obs[`i'] "," pct_nonmiss[`i']
}

title: Describing Data
text:
Aggregate statistics can conceal important variation across groups. For continuous variables, computing descriptives by subgroup makes it possible to compare, for instance, how disposable income differs across tenure statuses or demographic categories.
As seen in the section on categorical variables, collapse is a natural tool for this in Stata. Here the same logic applies, with (mean) as the descriptive measure of interest, though this can be replaced by any other statistic supported by the command, such as (median), (sd), or (p25) and (p75). The by() option ensures the computation is carried out separately for each combination of dataset and tenure group:


qui lissyuse, iso2(fr it es de) from(2021) hvars(hid dhi hwgt dname cname year own)
collapse (mean) avg_dhi = dhi, by(dname own cname year)
    
    decode own, gen(own_label)
    qui gen code = real(regexs(1)) if regexm(own_label, "\[([^\]]+)\]")
    qui gen label = substr(own_label, strpos(own_label, "]") + 1, .)


forvalues i = 1/`=_N' {
   if `i' == 1 {
     di "cname,year,code,label,avg_dhi"
        } 
     di cname[`i'] "," year[`i'] "," code[`i'] "," label[`i'] "," avg_dhi[`i'] 
}

  6. }

The two gen lines above handle a recurrent situation in LIS data. The variable own is originally numeric with value labels — category 110 is stored as the number 110 and displayed as owned outright. After decode, it becomes the plain string [110]owned outright. While readable, this single string is harder to filter or sort programmatically. The two lines split it back into its two components: code recovers the numeric part (110) by extracting the content inside the brackets, and label recovers the clean text (owned outright) by taking everything after the closing bracket. This gives you a tidy, analysis-ready output where the category code and its description live in separate variables.

title: Import Data
text:
LIS provides a downloadable file listing all available datasets in the LIS/LWS/LCS databases:
The file includes, among other information:

country codes,
available years,
survey names,
dataset identifiers, and
database membership (LIS/LWS/LCS).

It can be useful for quickly checking dataset availability or constructing loops programmatically in Stata.
A convenient way to inspect metadata information however, is by using the auxiliary functions provided in the R package lissyrtools as it offers more tailored searches directly within LISSY.

title: Import Data
text:
Finding variable names

its name in the dataset

Notes
Some variables are accompanied by notes. These may reflect:


changes in definition across years,


limitations in coverage,


the use of alternative weighting variables, or


other dataset-specific considerations highlighted by LIS.
