title: Structuring Results for Analysis
text:
In this final section, we build on the tabular structure introduced in the last section to produce visualizations in LISSY using R. We highlight a few particularities that users should be aware of when working in the LISSY environment, things that wouldn’t arise when coding locally. Our focus is exclusively on trends (line charts), organized around six templates that users can adapt to their own countries and variables of interest.
Working from templates matters more here than it would in a local session. LISSY operates on a job-submission system rather than an interactive one: there is no way to inspect intermediate output or tweak a chart on the fly, and every change requires a new submission. Starting from a tested example that already matches your use case significantly reduces the number of iterations needed.
Each template addresses a different combination of practical dimensions: the number of countries, the type of variable being plotted (a flow variable or a categorical one), the level of disaggregation, and the number of indicators shown simultaneously. Together they cover most situations a user is likely to encounter.
The six examples are organized as follows:


Examples 1–2 — single variable, one country or multiple countries (flow variable; categorical variable)

Examples 3–4 — categorical variable across multiple countries, with increasing disaggregation (standardized variable; country-specific variable)

Example 5 — standardized disaggregation by a person-level variable, multiple countries side by side

Example 6 — multiple derived indicators in a single plot, single country







Important



Unlike a local R session where plots render to screen, LISSY has no display — all output must be written to file. The png() function must be called before each plot. Without this, no chart is returned. When producing multiple figures in a single job, each png() call must use a unique filename — reusing a name will silently overwrite the earlier file and only the last chart will be recoverable. This is covered in detail in the png() section at the end.




This first template computes median equivalised disposable household income (dhi) over time for several countries simultaneously, expressed in PPP-adjusted 2021 US dollars. It illustrates the most common pattern: a flow variable aggregated to a single statistic per country-year, plotted as connected lines.
The lissyrtools pipeline handles the main transformations sequentially: IQR top and bottom coding to address extreme values, square-root equivalisation, PPP adjustment, and finally weighted percentile estimation. The result is passed directly to ggplot2 via lissyrtools::structure_to_plot() the functions resposible to restructure our data into a tidy data frame.

library(lissyrtools)
library(tidyverse)
library(scales)
library(labelled)


data_for_plot = lissyuse(
    data = c('fr', 'us', 'uk', 'lu', 'se'),
    'dhi',
    from = 2000,
    to = 2024,
    database = 'lis'
) %>%
    map(
        ~ .x %>% filter(!is.na(dhi)) %>% mutate(new_wgt = hwgt * nhhmem)
    ) %>%
    apply_iqr_top_bottom_coding('dhi', 'hwgt') %>%
    apply_sqrt_equivalisation('dhi') %>%
    apply_ppp_adjustment(
        'dhi',
        database = 'lis',
        transformation = 'lisppp',
        base_year_ppp = 2021
    ) %>%
    run_weighted_percentiles('dhi', 'new_wgt', probs = 0.5) %>%
    structure_to_plot()


 # Plot 

png(file = paste0(USR_PDF, "/ex.1.png"), width = 1280, height = 720, res = 150)

ggplot(data_for_plot, aes(x = year, y = value, group = cname, color = cname)) +
    geom_line() +
    geom_point(size = 2.5) +
    labs(
        x = "",
        y = "",
        title = "Median Disposable Household Income in US int.$ 2021",
        caption = "Source: Luxembourg Income Study"
    ) +
    scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
    scale_y_continuous(
        labels = comma,
        limits = c(0, NA),
        breaks = seq(0, 55000, by = 5000)
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
        panel.grid.major.y = element_line(linewidth = 0.3, color = "grey85"),
        panel.grid.minor.y = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor.x = element_blank(),
        legend.title = element_blank(),
        plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0, size = 8, color = "grey50"),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12)
    )




This template shifts from a flow variable to a categorical one. It plots the share of employment by industry sector (indb1) in Germany over time, using relative frequencies rather than a monetary aggregate. The data preparation is straightforward: lissyrtools::run_weighted_count() with percent = TRUE computes within-wave shares directly, and lissyrtools::structure_to_plot() reshapes the result for plotting.
This is a useful template for any LIS variable that takes a small number of discrete values and for which tracking compositional change over time is of interest (employment type, household structure, education level, and so on).






Note



Variable availability: Industry of employment is not available for all country-waves in LIS. Before running this template on a new country, check coverage in the LIS variable documentation, or using the methods described in the earlier chapters of this guide.



library(lissyrtools)
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)

data_for_plot = lissyuse(
    data = c('de'),
    'indb1',
    from = 2000,
    to = 2024,
    database = 'lis'
) %>%
    map(~ .x %>% filter(!is.na(indb1)))


png(
    file = paste0(USR_PDF, "/ex.2.png"),
    width = 1280,
    height = 720,
    res = 150
)

run_weighted_count(
    data_for_plot,
    var_name = "indb1",
    wgt_name = "ppopwgt",
    percent = TRUE
) %>%
    structure_to_plot() %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = year, y = value, group = category, color = category)) +
    geom_line() +
    geom_point(size = 2.5) +
    labs(
        x = "",
        y = "",
        title = "Employment by Industry Sector in Germany (2000–2024)",
        caption = "Source: Luxembourg Income Study"
    ) +
    scale_color_brewer(
        palette = "Paired",
        labels = \(x) str_wrap(x, width = 25)
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
        legend.position = "right",
        legend.title = element_blank(),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 8),
        legend.key.height = unit(1.5, "cm"),
        plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0, size = 8, color = "grey50"),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12)
    )




This template extends Example 2 to multiple countries, using occupation group (occa1) rather than industry. Rather than producing one plot per country and combining them manually, facet_wrap(~cname) handles the multi-country layout natively within a single ggplot2 call, producing side-by-side subplots with a shared legend.

library(lissyrtools)
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)

data_for_plot <- lissyuse(
    data = c('pe', 'lu'),
    'occa1',
    from = 2000,
    to = 2024,
    database = 'lis'
) %>%
    map(~ .x %>% filter(!is.na(occa1)))


png(file = paste0(USR_PDF, "/ex3.png"), width = 1280, height = 720, res = 150)

run_weighted_count(
    data_for_plot,
    var_name = "occa1",
    wgt_name = "ppopwgt",
    percent = TRUE
) %>%
    structure_to_plot() %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = year, y = value, group = category, color = category)) +
    geom_line() +
    geom_point(size = 2.5) +
    facet_wrap(~cname, ncol = 2) +
    labs(
        x = "",
        y = "",
        title = "Employment by Occupation Group (3 Categories)",
        caption = "Source: Luxembourg Income Study"
    ) +
    scale_color_brewer(
        palette = "Paired",
        labels = \(x) str_wrap(x, width = 20)
    ) +
    scale_y_continuous(
        breaks = scales::breaks_width(10)
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
        legend.position = "bottom",
        legend.title = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor.x = element_blank(),
        plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0, size = 8, color = "grey50"),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
        panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "grey85", linewidth = 0.5),
        panel.grid.minor = element_line(color = "grey85", linewidth = 0.3),
        panel.spacing = unit(1.5, "lines")
    )




The previous examples all used standardized LIS variables. This template instead uses region_c, a country-specific variable that is not harmonized across countries. The region filtering is applied after lissyrtools::structure_to_plot() using str_detect() on the category labels, selecting a meaningful subset of regions per country to keep the chart readable. The specific regions chosen here are illustrative.

library(lissyrtools)
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)


data_for_plot <- lissyuse(
    data = c('de', 'it'),
    c('dhi', 'region_c'),
    from = 2000,
    to = 2024,
    database = 'lis'
) %>%
    map(~ .x %>% filter(!is.na(dhi)) %>% mutate(new_wgt = nhhmem * hwgt)) %>%
    apply_iqr_top_bottom_coding('dhi', 'hwgt') %>%
    apply_sqrt_equivalisation('dhi') %>%
    apply_ppp_adjustment('dhi', database = 'lis', transformation = 'lisppp') %>%
    run_weighted_mean('dhi', 'new_wgt', by = 'region_c') %>%
    structure_to_plot() %>%
    filter(
        str_detect(
            category,
            paste(
                c(
                    'Lazio',
                    'Lombardia',
                    'Campania',
                    'Sicilia',
                    'Bavaria',
                    'Westphalia',
                    'Baden-Wuerttemberg',
                    'Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania'
                ),
                collapse = "|"
            )
        )
    )

png(file = paste0(USR_PDF, "/ex4.png"), width = 1280, height = 720, res = 150)

ggplot(
    data_for_plot,
    aes(x = year, y = value, group = category, color = category)
) +
    geom_line() +
    geom_point(size = 2.5) +
    facet_wrap(~cname, ncol = 2) +
    labs(
        x = "",
        y = "",
        title = "Mean Equivalised Disposable Income by Region",
        subtitle = "Germany and Italy, selected regions (CPI-adjusted, PPP)",
        caption = "Source: Luxembourg Income Study"
    ) +
    scale_color_brewer(
        palette = "Paired",
        labels = \(x) str_wrap(x, width = 20)
    ) +
    scale_y_continuous(
        labels = comma,
        ,
        limits = c(0, NA),
        breaks = seq(0, 50000, by = 5000)
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
        legend.position = "right",
        legend.title = element_blank(),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 8),
        legend.key.height = unit(1.5, "cm"),
        plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0, size = 8, color = "grey50"),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, color = "grey40"),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10)
    )




This template uses sex to disaggregate median labour income (pi11) for working-age employed individuals in Sweden and Germany. The sample is restricted to respondents aged 25–55 who are employed, a standard restriction for labour income analysis. facet_wrap("cname") handles the multi-country layout with a shared legend, and PPP adjustment is applied to express wages in comparable units across countries.

library(lissyrtools)
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)

lis_data <- lissyuse(
    data = c("se", "de"),
    vars = c("age", "sex", "pi11", "emp"),
    from = 2002
)


png(file = paste0(USR_PDF, "/ex5.png"), width = 1280, height = 720, res = 150)

lis_data %>%
    map(
        ~ .x %>%
            filter(age > 24 & age < 56) %>%
            filter(emp == 1) %>%
            filter(!is.na(pi11)) 
    ) %>%
    apply_ppp_adjustment(
        "pi11",
        database = "lis",
        transformation = "lisppp"
    ) %>%
    run_weighted_percentiles("pi11", "ppopwgt", probs = 0.5 , by = "sex") %>%
    structure_to_plot() %>%
    ggplot(
        aes(x = year, y = value, group = category, color = category)
    ) +
    geom_line() +
    geom_point(size = 2.5) +
    facet_wrap("cname") +
    labs(
        x = "",
        y = "",
        title = "Working-Age Median Wage",
        caption = "Source: Luxembourg Income Study",
        color = "Gender"
    ) +
    scale_y_continuous(
        labels = comma,
        limits = c(0, NA),
        breaks = seq(0, 60000, by = 5000)
    ) +
    scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
        legend.title = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "bottom",
        plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0, size = 8, color = "grey50"),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10)
    )     




The final template plots multiple derived indicators on the same axes and extends this to more than one country by producing one chart per country within the same job. Using the United Kingdom and Germany as examples, it computes three percentile ratios (90/10, 90/50, 50/10) of equivalised disposable income and plots them as a time series for each country in separate images.
The three ratios are computed separately using lissyrtools::run_weighted_ratios() and bound into a single data frame with a country and indicator identifier. An auxiliary function get_country_graph() then handles both the plot construction and the png() call for each country, keeping the final loop concise.






Important



Dynamic export naming: Because this template produces one chart per country within the same job submission, each png() call must use a unique filename. Here this is achieved inside get_country_graph() by embedding the country name directly in the path: paste0(USR_PDF, "/ratios_", country, ".png"). Without this, each iteration would overwrite the previous file and only the last country’s chart would be recoverable from LISSY output.



library(lissyrtools)
library(tidyverse)
library(ggpubr)
library(scales)


lis_datasets <- lissyuse(
    data = c("uk", "de"),
    vars = c("dhi"),
    from = 1970
)


ready_data <- lis_datasets %>%
    map(~ .x %>% filter(!is.na(dhi))) %>%
    apply_sqrt_equivalisation("dhi")


ratios <- bind_rows(
    # Ratio 90/10
    run_weighted_ratios(
        ready_data,
        var_name = "dhi",
        wgt_name = "hwgt",
        upper_percentile = 0.9,
        lower_percentile = 0.1
    ) %>%
        structure_to_plot() %>%
        mutate(indicator = "p_90_10"),
    # Ratio 90/50
    run_weighted_ratios(
        ready_data,
        var_name = "dhi",
        wgt_name = "hwgt",
        upper_percentile = 0.9,
        lower_percentile = 0.5
    ) %>%
        structure_to_plot() %>%
        mutate(indicator = "p_90_50"),
    # Ratio 50/10
    run_weighted_ratios(
        ready_data,
        var_name = "dhi",
        wgt_name = "hwgt",
        upper_percentile = 0.5,
        lower_percentile = 0.1
    ) %>%
        structure_to_plot() %>%
        mutate(indicator = "p_50_10")
)

# Auxilliary Printing Function
get_country_graph <- function(country) {
    p <- ggplot(
        ratios %>% filter(cname == country),
        aes(x = year, y = value, group = indicator, color = indicator)
    ) +
        geom_line() +
        geom_point(size = 2.5) +
        labs(
            x = "",
            y = "Ratio",
            title = paste0(country, " — Inequality Ratios"),
            caption = "Source: Luxembourg Income Study"
        ) +
        scale_y_continuous(
            labels = comma,
            limits = c(0, 5.5),
            breaks = seq(0, 6, by = 1)
        ) +
        scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
        theme_minimal() +
        theme(
            legend.position = "right",
            legend.title = element_blank(),
            plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0, size = 8, color = "grey50"),
            plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12)
        )

    fileName <- paste0(USR_PDF, "/ratios_", country, ".png")

    print(png(file = fileName, width = 1280, height = 720, res = 150))
    print(p)
}


# Final Loop per Country
countries <- unique(ratios$cname)
for (country in countries) {
    get_country_graph(country)
}




In a standard R session, plots render directly to screen. In LISSY, there is no display — all output must be written to file. The png() function serves this purpose, and its correct use is essential for any visualization job.
It controls two things:


Output filename: The file argument defines where the chart is saved. Always write to USR_PDF, the LISSY-provided path for user output files.

Plot dimensions and resolution: The width, height, and res arguments control the pixel dimensions and dots-per-inch of the exported image. The values used throughout these examples (width = 1280, height = 720, res = 150) produce a 1280×720px image at 150 DPI, which renders clearly in most contexts.







Important



Unique filenames are mandatory when producing multiple plots in one job. Each png() call opens a new graphics device writing to the specified path. If two calls share the same filename, the second will overwrite the first, and only the last chart will be recoverable from LISSY output. Use descriptive, numbered, or otherwise distinct names — as done throughout these examples — whenever a single job produces more than one figure.

title: Structuring Results for Analysis
text:
This first template computes median equivalised disposable household income (dhi) over time for several countries simultaneously, expressed in PPP-adjusted 2021 US dollars. It illustrates the most common pattern: a flow variable aggregated to a single statistic per country-year, plotted as connected lines.
The lissyrtools pipeline handles the main transformations sequentially: IQR top and bottom coding to address extreme values, square-root equivalisation, PPP adjustment, and finally weighted percentile estimation. The result is passed directly to ggplot2 via lissyrtools::structure_to_plot() the functions resposible to restructure our data into a tidy data frame.

library(lissyrtools)
library(tidyverse)
library(scales)
library(labelled)


data_for_plot = lissyuse(
    data = c('fr', 'us', 'uk', 'lu', 'se'),
    'dhi',
    from = 2000,
    to = 2024,
    database = 'lis'
) %>%
    map(
        ~ .x %>% filter(!is.na(dhi)) %>% mutate(new_wgt = hwgt * nhhmem)
    ) %>%
    apply_iqr_top_bottom_coding('dhi', 'hwgt') %>%
    apply_sqrt_equivalisation('dhi') %>%
    apply_ppp_adjustment(
        'dhi',
        database = 'lis',
        transformation = 'lisppp',
        base_year_ppp = 2021
    ) %>%
    run_weighted_percentiles('dhi', 'new_wgt', probs = 0.5) %>%
    structure_to_plot()


 # Plot 

png(file = paste0(USR_PDF, "/ex.1.png"), width = 1280, height = 720, res = 150)

ggplot(data_for_plot, aes(x = year, y = value, group = cname, color = cname)) +
    geom_line() +
    geom_point(size = 2.5) +
    labs(
        x = "",
        y = "",
        title = "Median Disposable Household Income in US int.$ 2021",
        caption = "Source: Luxembourg Income Study"
    ) +
    scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
    scale_y_continuous(
        labels = comma,
        limits = c(0, NA),
        breaks = seq(0, 55000, by = 5000)
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
        panel.grid.major.y = element_line(linewidth = 0.3, color = "grey85"),
        panel.grid.minor.y = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor.x = element_blank(),
        legend.title = element_blank(),
        plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0, size = 8, color = "grey50"),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12)
    )

title: Structuring Results for Analysis
text:
This template shifts from a flow variable to a categorical one. It plots the share of employment by industry sector (indb1) in Germany over time, using relative frequencies rather than a monetary aggregate. The data preparation is straightforward: lissyrtools::run_weighted_count() with percent = TRUE computes within-wave shares directly, and lissyrtools::structure_to_plot() reshapes the result for plotting.
This is a useful template for any LIS variable that takes a small number of discrete values and for which tracking compositional change over time is of interest (employment type, household structure, education level, and so on).






Note



Variable availability: Industry of employment is not available for all country-waves in LIS. Before running this template on a new country, check coverage in the LIS variable documentation, or using the methods described in the earlier chapters of this guide.



library(lissyrtools)
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)

data_for_plot = lissyuse(
    data = c('de'),
    'indb1',
    from = 2000,
    to = 2024,
    database = 'lis'
) %>%
    map(~ .x %>% filter(!is.na(indb1)))


png(
    file = paste0(USR_PDF, "/ex.2.png"),
    width = 1280,
    height = 720,
    res = 150
)

run_weighted_count(
    data_for_plot,
    var_name = "indb1",
    wgt_name = "ppopwgt",
    percent = TRUE
) %>%
    structure_to_plot() %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = year, y = value, group = category, color = category)) +
    geom_line() +
    geom_point(size = 2.5) +
    labs(
        x = "",
        y = "",
        title = "Employment by Industry Sector in Germany (2000–2024)",
        caption = "Source: Luxembourg Income Study"
    ) +
    scale_color_brewer(
        palette = "Paired",
        labels = \(x) str_wrap(x, width = 25)
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
        legend.position = "right",
        legend.title = element_blank(),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 8),
        legend.key.height = unit(1.5, "cm"),
        plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0, size = 8, color = "grey50"),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12)
    )

title: Structuring Results for Analysis
text:

title: Structuring Results for Analysis
text:
The previous examples all used standardized LIS variables. This template instead uses region_c, a country-specific variable that is not harmonized across countries. The region filtering is applied after lissyrtools::structure_to_plot() using str_detect() on the category labels, selecting a meaningful subset of regions per country to keep the chart readable. The specific regions chosen here are illustrative.

library(lissyrtools)
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)


data_for_plot <- lissyuse(
    data = c('de', 'it'),
    c('dhi', 'region_c'),
    from = 2000,
    to = 2024,
    database = 'lis'
) %>%
    map(~ .x %>% filter(!is.na(dhi)) %>% mutate(new_wgt = nhhmem * hwgt)) %>%
    apply_iqr_top_bottom_coding('dhi', 'hwgt') %>%
    apply_sqrt_equivalisation('dhi') %>%
    apply_ppp_adjustment('dhi', database = 'lis', transformation = 'lisppp') %>%
    run_weighted_mean('dhi', 'new_wgt', by = 'region_c') %>%
    structure_to_plot() %>%
    filter(
        str_detect(
            category,
            paste(
                c(
                    'Lazio',
                    'Lombardia',
                    'Campania',
                    'Sicilia',
                    'Bavaria',
                    'Westphalia',
                    'Baden-Wuerttemberg',
                    'Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania'
                ),
                collapse = "|"
            )
        )
    )

png(file = paste0(USR_PDF, "/ex4.png"), width = 1280, height = 720, res = 150)

ggplot(
    data_for_plot,
    aes(x = year, y = value, group = category, color = category)
) +
    geom_line() +
    geom_point(size = 2.5) +
    facet_wrap(~cname, ncol = 2) +

        labels = comma,
        ,
        limits = c(0, NA),
        breaks = seq(0, 50000, by = 5000)
    ) +

    theme(
        legend.position = "right",
        legend.title = element_blank(),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 8),

title: Structuring Results for Analysis
text:
This template uses sex to disaggregate median labour income (pi11) for working-age employed individuals in Sweden and Germany. The sample is restricted to respondents aged 25–55 who are employed, a standard restriction for labour income analysis. facet_wrap("cname") handles the multi-country layout with a shared legend, and PPP adjustment is applied to express wages in comparable units across countries.

library(lissyrtools)
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)

lis_data <- lissyuse(
    data = c("se", "de"),
    vars = c("age", "sex", "pi11", "emp"),
    from = 2002
)


png(file = paste0(USR_PDF, "/ex5.png"), width = 1280, height = 720, res = 150)

lis_data %>%
    map(
        ~ .x %>%
            filter(age > 24 & age < 56) %>%
            filter(emp == 1) %>%
            filter(!is.na(pi11)) 
    ) %>%
    apply_ppp_adjustment(
        "pi11",
        database = "lis",
        transformation = "lisppp"
    ) %>%
    run_weighted_percentiles("pi11", "ppopwgt", probs = 0.5 , by = "sex") %>%
    structure_to_plot() %>%
    ggplot(
        aes(x = year, y = value, group = category, color = category)
    ) +
    geom_line() +
    geom_point(size = 2.5) +
    facet_wrap("cname") +
    labs(
        x = "",
        y = "",
        title = "Working-Age Median Wage",
        caption = "Source: Luxembourg Income Study",
        color = "Gender"
    ) +
    scale_y_continuous(
        labels = comma,
        limits = c(0, NA),
        breaks = seq(0, 60000, by = 5000)
    ) +
    scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
        legend.title = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "bottom",
        plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0, size = 8, color = "grey50"),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10)
    )

title: Import Data
text:
As discussed earlier, the remainder of this guide focuses on Method 1, which imports LIS data as a list. In this structure, each element corresponds to a dataset for a specific country–year combination, at either the household or person level.
This approach reflects the way LIS data are organized and makes it possible to work with multiple datasets in a consistent and transparent manner.


While the choice ultimately depends on user preference and the specific task at hand, there are several reasons why keeping the data in a list structure may be more appropriate.


Given the way lissyrtools is designed, it is often more effective to retain the original list structure returned by lissyuse(). In general, many functions in the package are built around list-based workflows and functional programming principles, which are used consistently throughout this guide.
Working with a list of data frames removes the need to explicitly loop over each country–year (ccyy) dataset when applying common transformations. For example, operations such as top- or bottom-coding based on distributional criteria can be applied seamlessly across all elements of the list.
Similarly, there is no need to manually merge auxiliary data such as deflators or PPP conversion factors. Functions like apply_ppp_adjustment() handle these operations directly, applying the appropriate transformation to each country–year dataset within the list.
In addition, lissyrtools provides a range of functions to compute survey-weighted indicators of inequality and poverty. These functions automatically return results aggregated by country and year, and, when relevant, by categories, with the option to further disaggregate by additional subgroups. This reduces the need for explicit grouping operations using functions such as group_by().
Overall, this approach supports a workflow that is more efficient, more readable, more reproducible, and less prone to error.


What if lissyrtools does not porvide a specific functionality required for the analysis? This is where the purrr package, part of the tidyverse, becomes particularly useful.
As comprehensive as it is, lissyrtools cannot account for all possible adjustments that a user may wish to implement. In such cases, it may be necessary to rely on more flexible tools such as those provided in purrr.
One of the most intuitive ways to work with lists is to first define a data-processing pipeline for a single data frame, and then generalize that pipeline to all elements of the list using functions like purrr::map(). This approach, commonly referred to as functional programming (FP), allows for clear and readable code, while ensuring that the same transformations (functions) are applied consistently across all datasets.
The examples below illustrate actions coded inside purrr functions such as:

recoding a categorical variable,
filtering out missing values, and
applying transformations only to a subset of data frames.


lissyrtools::lissyuse(c('es16', 'it16'), vars = c('dhi', 'sex')) %>%
  purrr::map(
    ~ .x %>% # '.x' represents an element of the list. A data frame in this case
      dplyr::mutate(
        sex_lis_variable = sex,
        sex = dplyr::case_when(
          sex == 1 ~ 0,
          sex == 2 ~ 1,
          is.na(sex) ~ TRUE
        )
      ) %>%
      filter(!is.na(dhi))
  )


lissyrtools::lissyuse(c("es16", "it16"), vars = c("dhi", "sex", 'iso3')) %>%
  purrr::imap(
    ~ if (stringr::str_starts(.y, 'es')) { # '.y' represents the name of an element on the list.
      .x %>% dplyr::mutate(iso2 = 'sp')
    } else {
      .x
    }
  )

In this guide, three key functions from this package will be addressed. These are: purrr::map(), purrr::imap() and purrr::map2().


Another key reason to avoid immediately combining datasets is the presence of country-specific variables.
These variables, identified by the _c suffix (e.g. region_c, ethnic_c), are not directly comparable across countries. This is due either to:

the nature of the concepts they capture (such as geography or education systems)
differences in the classifications used by national data providers (e.g. labor market occupation or economic activity classifications), which may not follow a common international standard.

As a result, although these variables share the same name across datasets, their underlying numeric codes and associated labels can differ across countries, and in some cases even across years within the same country.
The image below illustrates a case where an Italian and a German region share the same numeric code:




Binding these datasets together immediately, can therefore lead to label conflicts, as illustrated in the example below.

library(lissyrtools)
library(dplyr)

x <- lissyuse(
  data = c("it16", "de16"), 
  vars = "region_c"
  )

x_binded <- dplyr::bind_rows(x)

Warning: `..1$region_c` and `..2$region_c` have conflicting value labels.
ℹ Labels for these values will be taken from `..1$region_c`.
✖ Values: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, …, 15, and 16


Keeping datasets in a list helps preserve these differences and avoids unintended inconsistencies. Lists in R therefore provide a flexible way to organize LIS data while still allowing us to apply the same operations to each dataset.

We also highlighted the benefits of working with lists in R, and showed how to work around current limitations of lissyrtools. In the next section, we shift focus to a more hands-on exploration on how to get quickly acquainted with the data imported.

title: Data Handling
text:
Currency and Price Level Adjustments
LIS variables on income, wealth, and consumption are always expressed in national currency at current prices for that income reference year. While this preserves the data in a form close to its original source, it also creates clear comparability issues across countries.
For clarity, the snippet below retrieves the unweighted average of disposable household income (dhi) for both the United States and Sweden in 2018.

library(lissyrtools)
library(dplyr)

lissyuse(data = c('us18', 'se18'), vars  = 'dhi') %>% 
    run_weighted_mean('dhi')

The list contains the following `household-level` data frames: se18h, us18h.


 
$Sweden
    2018 
504749.2 

$`United States`
    2018 
73735.58 





The figures reported above are not directly comparable. The large difference in magnitude, wtih Sweden appearing to have values more than five times higher than those of the United States, does not reflect real differences in income levels, but rather the fact that the data are expressed in different national currencies, implying the need for additional transformation steps.
To address this issue, LIS provides both CPI and PPP deflators for each country and year. These allow users to convert values into a common, comparable scale. In practice, this process is simplified through the lissyrtools::apply_ppp_adjustment() function, which automatically applies the necessary transformations and enables meaningful comparisons across countries and over time.




As shown in the example above, we have 3 columns with conversion factors that the user can make use of. These are:

Consumer Price Index: needed to compare real amounts over time within countries;
Purchasing Power Parity: needed to compare real amounts across countries;
LISPPP: which combine CPI and PPP deflators and can be used to compare real amounts across countries and over time.

Once equipped with these tools and resources we can now redo the exercise above by making use of the PPP conversion factors, by specifying it, in the form of a character, in the transformation argument.

lissyuse(data = c('us18', 'se18'), vars  = 'dhi') %>% 
    apply_ppp_adjustment(
        var_name = 'dhi', 
        database = 'lis', 
        transformation = 'ppp', 
        base_year_ppp = 2021
        ) %>% 
    run_weighted_mean('dhi')

Variable 'dhi' was adjusted for cross-country comparability using '2021' USD PPP conversion factors (USA = 1).


$Sweden
    2018 
55795.59 

$`United States`
    2018 
73735.58 





The Swedish figure is now much closer to American one, as both are expressed in international US dollars at 2021 prices. This adjustment makes the values directly comparable and better reflects real income levels.






Warning



In some LWS datasets, wealth amounts and income amounts might differ in their reference year. The year of the dataset always corresponds to the wealth amounts reference year, but income amounts might have been expresssed as the ones in the year before. LWS data users, do not need to worry with this as long as they mannualy specify database = 'lws', which immediately adjust the reference year depending on var_name is a wealth (dnw) or income variable (dhi).


To conclude this section on adjusting data for differences in currency and price levels, we present two additional examples illustrating how CPI and LISPPP deflators can be used in practice.
We begin with a case where the analysis focuses on a single country. In such situations, users may wish to keep results expressed in the country’s national currency while adjusting for inflation over time. Applying the CPI deflator allows values to be converted into constant prices, ensuring that changes reflect real variation rather than shifts in the price level.

lissyuse(data = 'it', vars  = 'dhi', from = 2010) %>%  
    run_weighted_mean('dhi')

 
$Italy
    2022     2020     2016     2014     2012     2010 
46301.93 48072.00 24881.99 25444.73 25853.37 26647.06 






lissyuse(data = 'it', vars  = 'dhi', from = 2010) %>%  
    apply_ppp_adjustment(
        var_name = 'dhi', 
        database = 'lis', 
        transformation = 'cpi',  
        base_year_ppp = 2021
        ) %>% 
    run_weighted_mean('dhi')

Variable 'dhi' was adjusted for domestic inflation using the CPI (base year '2021' = 100).


 
$Italy
    2022     2020     2016     2014     2012     2010 
42792.40 48972.77 26073.67 26648.62 27472.99 29988.93 






Alternatively, users may be interested in making comparisons across countries and over time. In this context, relying solely on CPI adjustments is not sufficient, as values would still be expressed in different national currencies. This is where the LISPPP deflator becomes particularly useful. By combining both CPI and PPP adjustments, it converts values into a international US dollars at a given base year, thereby enabling meaningful cross-country comparisons in real terms.

lissyuse(data = c('it', 'se'), vars = 'dhi', from = 2010) %>%
    run_weighted_mean('dhi')

 
$Italy
    2022     2020     2016     2014     2012     2010 
46301.93 48072.00 24881.99 25444.73 25853.37 26647.06 

$Sweden
    2023     2022     2021     2020     2019     2018     2017     2016 
638771.3 601107.7 575956.5 546580.8 534309.5 504749.2 509026.1 505105.1 
    2015     2014     2013     2012     2011     2010 
478623.5 464035.1 446265.0 440190.5 586478.0 665450.7 






lissyuse(data = c('it', 'se'), vars  = 'dhi', from = 2010) %>%  
    apply_ppp_adjustment(
        var_name = 'dhi', 
        database = 'lis', 
        transformation = 'lisppp',
        base_year_ppp = 2021) %>% 
    run_weighted_mean('dhi') 

Variable 'dhi' was adjusted using LIS-specific deflators: both for domestic inflation (CPI, base year '2021' = 100), and for cross-country comparability using purchasing power parity (PPP) conversion factors, with '2021' USD as the base (USA = 1).


 
$Italy
    2022     2020     2016     2014     2012     2010 
61138.98 69969.09 37252.36 38073.81 39251.62 42846.23 

$Sweden
    2023     2022     2021     2020     2019     2018     2017     2016 
60025.95 61315.50 63666.93 61726.71 60641.00 58308.14 59950.93 60556.66 
    2015     2014     2013     2012     2011     2010 
57946.59 56154.11 53906.68 53149.37 71441.45 83461.82 





Together, these approaches highlight the importance of selecting the appropriate deflator depending on the analytical objective, whether the focus is on within-country trends or cross-country comparability.

The sections that follow illustrates a more comprehensive workflow, combining several preparation steps to construct a policy-relevant indicator from microdata.
The aim will be to compute the poverty rate among children in single-mother households in the United States. Constructing this indicator requires combining information available at both the household level (dhi, nhhmem17, hpartner), and the individual level (sex).






Important



Recall from the early sections of this guidebook when we introduced lissyuse(), that when both household and individual levels are specified in vars, both files for a given ccyy are loaded are merged automatically. Therefore we end up with the data loaded at the individual level.



us_data <- lissyuse(
  data = "us",  
  vars = c("dhi", "nhhmem17", "sex", "hpartner"), # 3 'h-level' + 1 'p-level'
  from = 2018, 
  to = 2024   
)  

The list contains the following `person-level` data frames: us24, us23, us22, us21, us20, us19, us18.








Note



Variables relation and nhhmem are part of the group of variables that are always imported by default.


{r,  class.output = "foldable"},  columns = names(us_data[[1]]) lissyrtools::variable_labels(vars = columns)


At this stage, we prepare the dataset so that it is aligned with the unit of analysis required for our indicator: the household. Although we imported both household- and person-level variables, the poverty measure is computed at the household level and then attributed to individuals (in this case, children).

data_prep <- us_data %>%
  purrr::map(~ .x %>% 
        filter(!is.na(dhi)) %>% 
        filter(relation == 1000) %>% 
        mutate(
          new_wgt = hwgt * nhhmem,
          new_chld_wgt = hwgt * nhhmem17,
        )
  )

Like in previous examples, we will define a pipeline inside the purrr::map() function to apply the same processes for each dataset. We begin by filtering out observations with missing disposable household income (dhi). Next, we retain only records corresponding to the household reference person (relation == 1000). This step ensures that each household appears only once in the dataset, avoiding duplication that would arise from person-level records.
We then construct adjusted weights. For population-level indicators, we use a person-level weight derived from the household weight multiplied by household size (hwgt * nhhmem). For child-specific indicators, we instead construct a child weight by multiplying the household weight by the number of children in the household (hwgt * nhhmem17). These weights ensure that estimates correctly reflect the underlying population structure.


Before proceeding with inequality and poverty calculations, we address the presence of extreme income values. While the underlying microdata do not impose bounds on income, very high or very low values can disproportionately influence distributional measures.
To mitigate this, we apply bottom- and top-coding to disposable household income (dhi), with the help of another auxilliary function named apply_iqr_top_bottom_coding() tailored specifically for such stage.

data_tb_coded <- data_prep %>%
    lissyrtools::apply_iqr_top_bottom_coding(
        var_name = 'dhi', 
        wgt_name = 'hwgt', 
        times = 3, 
        one_sided = NULL,
        type = 'type_4' 
        )

In more detail, this adjustment is carried out on the logarithmic scale using an interquartile range (IQR) rule: values above the upper threshold (Q3 + 3×IQR) are capped, and values below the lower threshold (Q1 − 3×IQR) are raised. This method ensures that extreme observations do not disproportionately affect the results, while preserving the overall shape and structure of the income distribution.






Note



To ensure consistency with the latest methodology applied by LIS across all disseminated aggregate figures, this step must be performed prior to equivalisation. In addition, the quartiles used to define the IQR thresholds should be estimated following Definition 4 as proposed by Hyndman and Fan (1996).





Households differ in size and composition, which affects their economic needs. To enable meaningful comparisons across households, we equivalize disposable household income.
We apply the square root equivalence scale, dividing household income by the square root of the total number of household members. This transformation accounts for economies of scale in consumption: larger households require more resources, but not proportionally more per additional member.
As a result, all individuals within a household are assigned the same equivalised income, regardless of their age or role within the household.

data_eqv <- data_tb_coded %>%
     lissyrtools::apply_sqrt_equivalisation(
        var_name = 'dhi'
        )



At this point, we have done all the adjustments to original dhi variable, and reduced the dataset to the household-level. We are now settled to compute a poverty line that we will establish to be 50% of the weighted median of equivalised income
We can use the already familiar run_weighted_percentiles() that by default will compute the Minimum the Maximum and the 25th, 50th and 75th percentiles, and output themn in a named vector inside a list.

lissyrtools::run_weighted_percentiles(
        data_eqv[1], 
        var_name = "dhi", 
        wgt_name = "new_wgt"
    )

$us24
          0%          25%          50%          75%         100% 
    362.2004   31148.7992   51944.4144   81552.4012 1099114.7599 


Therefore, we can use the map() function and retreive only the elemet corresponding to the Median, named “50%”, and then multiply it by 0.5 to establish the poverty line. This relative definition ensures that poverty is assessed in relation to the living standards prevailing within each dataset, and thus there is no need to adjust for inflation or for diffferent currencies.

medians <- purrr::map(
    lissyrtools::run_weighted_percentiles(
        data_eqv, 
        var_name = "dhi", 
        wgt_name = "new_wgt"
    ), "50%"
)
poverty_lines <- purrr::map(medians  , ~ .x  * 0.5) # Half of the Median

print(poverty_lines)

$us24
[1] 25972.21

$us23
[1] 24599.92

$us22
[1] 22910.16

$us21
[1] 23328.8

$us20
[1] 22156.97

$us19
[1] 20941.03

$us18
[1] 19427.36


It is important to note that poverty lines are always calculated based on the full population. These same thresholds are subsequently used when evaluating poverty rates for specific subgroups, such as children or the elderly.


With the poverty line established, we create an indicator identifying whether each household falls below this threshold. For each observation, we compare equivalised income (dhi) to the poverty line.
Households with income below the threshold are classified as poor and assigned a value of 100, while all others are assigned 0. This binary indicator forms the basis for computing poverty rates.

data_with_pov_line <- purrr::map2(
  data_eqv,
  poverty_lines,
  ~ .x %>%
    dplyr::mutate(
      line = .y,
      poor = dplyr::if_else(dhi < line, 100, 0)
    )
)







Tip



When using purrr::map()2, ‘.x’ refers to the first element of the first list data_eqv, whilst ‘.y’ to the first element of the second list povery_lines.


By expressing the indicator as 0/100 rather than 0/1, the resulting weighted mean directly corresponds to a percentage.


In the final step, we restrict the sample to the population of interest: children living in single-mother households. This is defined as households where the reference person is female (sex == 2), has no partner present (hpartner == 0), and where at least one child is present (nhhmem17 > 0).
We then compute the weighted mean of the poverty indicator using the child-specific weight (hwgt * nhhmem17). This produces the poverty rate among children in single-mother households.
Throughout this process, the poverty line remains fixed—having been calculated for the total population—while the weighting scheme ensures that the estimate accurately reflects the distribution of children across households.

data_with_pov_line %>% 
  purrr::map( ~ .x %>%
         filter(hpartner==0 & sex==2 & nhhmem17>0)
  ) %>% 
  run_weighted_mean("poor", "new_chld_wgt")

title: Data Handling
text:
Income, wealth, and consumption data provided by LIS are expressed in national currencies at current prices for the income reference year. While this preserves the data in a form close to its original source, it also creates clear comparability issues across countries.
For clarity, the snippet below retrieves the unweighted average of disposable household income (dhi) for both the United States and Sweden in 2018.

library(lissyrtools)
library(dplyr)

lissyuse(data = c('us18', 'se18'), vars  = 'dhi') %>% 
    run_weighted_mean('dhi')

The list contains the following `household-level` data frames: se18h, us18h.


 
$Sweden
    2018 
504749.2 

$`United States`
    2018 
73735.58 





The figures reported above are not directly comparable. The large difference in magnitude, wtih Sweden appearing to have values more than five times higher than those of the United States, does not reflect real differences in income levels, but rather the fact that the data are expressed in different national currencies, implying the need for additional transformation steps.
To address this issue, LIS provides both CPI and PPP deflators for each country and year. These allow users to convert values into a common, comparable scale. In practice, this process is simplified through the lissyrtools::apply_ppp_adjustment() function, which automatically applies the necessary transformations and enables meaningful comparisons across countries and over time.




As shown in the example above, we have 3 columns with conversion factors that the user can make use of. These are:

Consummer Price Index: needed to compare real amounts over time within countries;
Purchasing Power Parity: needed to compare real amounts across countries;
LISPPP: which combine CPI and PPP deflators and can be used to compare real amounts across countries and over time.

Once equipped with these tools and resources we can now redo the exercise above by making use of the PPP conversion factors, by specifying it, in the form of a character, in the transformation argument.

lissyuse(data = c('us18', 'se18'), vars  = 'dhi') %>% 
    apply_ppp_adjustment(
        var_name = 'dhi', 
        database = 'lis', 
        transformation = 'ppp', 
        base_year_ppp = 2021
        ) %>% 
    run_weighted_mean('dhi')

Variable 'dhi' was adjusted for cross-country comparability using '2021' USD PPP conversion factors (USA = 1).


$Sweden
    2018 
55795.59 

$`United States`
    2018 
73735.58 





The Swedish figure is now much closer to American one, as both are expressed in international US dollars at 2021 prices. This adjustment makes the values directly comparable and better reflects real income levels.






Warning



In some LWS datasets, wealth amounts and income amounts might differ in their reference year. The year odf the dataset always corresponds to the wealth amounts reference year, but income amounts might have been expresssed as the ones in the year before. LWS data users, do not need to worry with this as long as they mannualy sprecify database = 'lws', which immediately adjust the reference year depending on var_name is a wealth (dnw) or income variable (dhi).


To conclude this section on adjusting data for differences in currency and price levels, we present two additional examples illustrating how CPI and LISPPP deflators can be used in practice.
We begin with a case where the analysis focuses on a single country. In such situations, users may wish to keep results expressed in the country’s national currency while adjusting for inflation over time. Applying the CPI deflator allows values to be converted into constant prices, ensuring that changes reflect real variation rather than shifts in the price level.

lissyuse(data = 'it', vars  = 'dhi', from = 2010) %>%  
    run_weighted_mean('dhi')

        base_year_ppp = 2021

By combining both CPI and PPP adjustments, it converts values into a international US dollars at a given base year, thereby enabling meaningful cross-country comparisons in real terms.

The sections that follow illustrates a more comprehensive workflow, combining several preparation steps to construct a policy-relevant indicator from microdata.
The aim will be to compute the poverty rate among children in single-mother households in the United States. Constructing this indicator requires combining information available at both the household level (dhi, nhhmem17, hpartner), and the individual level (sex).






Important



Recall from the early sections of this guidebook when we introduced lissyuse(), that when both household and individual levels are specified in vars, both files for a given ccyy are loaded are merged automatically. Therefore we end up with the data loaded at the individual level.



us_data <- lissyuse(
  data = "us",  
  vars = c("dhi", "nhhmem17", "sex", "hpartner"), # 3 'h-level' + 1 'p-level'
  from = 2018, 
  to = 2024   
)  

The list contains the following `person-level` data frames: us24, us23, us22, us21, us20, us19, us18.








Note



Variables relation and nhhmem are part of the group of variables that are always imported by default.


{r,  class.output = "foldable"},  columns = names(us_data[[1]]) lissyrtools::variable_labels(vars = columns)

title: Data Handling
text:
At this stage, we prepare the dataset so that it is aligned with the unit of analysis required for our indicator: the household. Although we imported both household- and person-level variables, the poverty measure is computed at the household level and then attributed to individuals (in this case, children).

data_prep <- us_data %>%
  purrr::map(~ .x %>% 
        filter(!is.na(dhi)) %>% 
        filter(relation == 1000) %>% 
        mutate(
          new_wgt = hwgt * nhhmem,
          new_chld_wgt = hwgt * nhhmem17,
        )
  )

Like in previous examples, we will define a pipeline inside the purrr::map() function to apply the same processes for each dataset. We begin by filtering out observations with missing disposable household income (dhi). Next, we retain only records corresponding to the household reference person (relation == 1000). This step ensures that each household appears only once in the dataset, avoiding duplication that would arise from person-level records.
We then construct adjusted weights. For population-level indicators, we use a person-level weight derived from the household weight multiplied by household size (hwgt * nhhmem). For child-specific indicators, we instead construct a child weight by multiplying the household weight by the number of children in the household (hwgt * nhhmem17). These weights ensure that estimates correctly reflect the underlying population structure.

title: Data Handling
text:
Before proceeding with inequality and poverty calculations, we address the presence of extreme income values. While the underlying microdata do not impose bounds on income, very high or very low values can disproportionately influence distributional measures.
To mitigate this, we apply bottom- and top-coding to disposable household income (dhi), with the help of another auxilliary function named apply_iqr_top_bottom_coding() tailored specifically for such stage.

data_tb_coded <- data_prep %>%
    lissyrtools::apply_iqr_top_bottom_coding(
        var_name = 'dhi', 
        wgt_name = 'hwgt', 
        times = 3, 
        one_sided = NULL,
        type = 'type_4' 
        )

In more detail, this adjustment is carried out on the logarithmic scale using an interquartile range (IQR) rule: values above the upper threshold (Q3 + 3×IQR) are capped, and values below the lower threshold (Q1 − 3×IQR) are raised. This method ensures that extreme observations do not disproportionately affect the results, while preserving the overall shape and structure of the income distribution.






Note



To ensure consistency with the latest methodology applied by LIS across all disseminated aggregate figures, this step must be performed prior to equivalisation. In addition, the quartiles used to define the IQR thresholds should be estimated following Definition 4 as proposed by Hyndman and Fan (1996).

title: Data Handling
text:
Households differ in size and composition, which affects their economic needs. To enable meaningful comparisons across households, we equivalize disposable household income.
We apply the square root equivalence scale, dividing household income by the square root of the total number of household members. This transformation accounts for economies of scale in consumption: larger households require more resources, but not proportionally more per additional member.
As a result, all individuals within a household are assigned the same equivalised income, regardless of their age or role within the household.

data_eqv <- data_tb_coded %>%
     lissyrtools::apply_sqrt_equivalisation(
        var_name = 'dhi'
        )

title: Data Handling
text:
At this point, we have done all the adjustments to original dhi variable, and reduced the dataset to the household-level. We are now settled to compute a poverty line that we will establish to be 50% of the weighted median of equivalised income
We can use the already familiar run_weighted_percentiles() that by default will compute the Minimum the Maximum and the 25th, 50th and 75th percentiles, and output themn in a named vector inside a list.

lissyrtools::run_weighted_percentiles(
        data_eqv[1], 
        var_name = "dhi", 
        wgt_name = "new_wgt"
    )

$us24
          0%          25%          50%          75%         100% 
    362.2004   31148.7992   51944.4144   81552.4012 1099114.7599 


Therefore, we can use the map() function and retreive only the elemet corresponding to the Median, named “50%”, and then multiply it by 0.5 to establish the poverty line. This relative definition ensures that poverty is assessed in relation to the living standards prevailing within each dataset, and thus there is no need to adjust for inflation or for diffferent currencies.

medians <- purrr::map(
    lissyrtools::run_weighted_percentiles(
        data_eqv, 
        var_name = "dhi", 
        wgt_name = "new_wgt"
    ), "50%"
)
poverty_lines <- purrr::map(medians  , ~ .x  * 0.5) # Half of the Median

print(poverty_lines)

It is important to note that poverty lines are always calculated based on the full population. These same thresholds are subsequently used when evaluating poverty rates for specific subgroups, such as children or the elderly.

title: Data Handling
text:
With the poverty line established, we create an indicator identifying whether each household falls below this threshold. For each observation, we compare equivalised income (dhi) to the poverty line.
Households with income below the threshold are classified as poor and assigned a value of 100, while all others are assigned 0. This binary indicator forms the basis for computing poverty rates.

data_with_pov_line <- purrr::map2(
  data_eqv,
  poverty_lines,
  ~ .x %>%
    dplyr::mutate(
      line = .y,
      poor = dplyr::if_else(dhi < line, 100, 0)
    )
)

When using purrr::map()2, ‘.x’ refers to the first element of the first list data_eqv, whilst ‘.y’ to the first element of the second list povery_lines.


By expressing the indicator as 0/100 rather than 0/1, the resulting weighted mean directly corresponds to a percentage.

We then compute the weighted mean of the poverty indicator using the child-specific weight (hwgt * nhhmem17). This produces the poverty rate among children in single-mother households.
Throughout this process, the poverty line remains fixed—having been calculated for the total population—while the weighting scheme ensures that the estimate accurately reflects the distribution of children across households.

         filter(hpartner==0 & sex==2 & nhhmem17>0)
  ) %>%

title: Describing Data
text:
In LIS, LWS and LCS datasets, continuous variables are distinct from the socioeconomic categorical variables discussed in the previous section. Rather than grouping households or individuals into discrete classes, they capture actual flows and stocks — income, consumption, and wealth, along with their subcomponents and aggregates. Examples include disposable household income (dhi), capital income (hicapital), and net worth (dnw). These variables tend to be right-skewed, can span several orders of magnitude, and vary considerably in coverage across country-years — a variable that is well-populated in one dataset may be sparse or entirely absent in another. Getting a quick distributional snapshot before any substantive analysis is therefore good practice. The emphasis in this section is not so much on the mechanics of any single statistic, but on building reproducible workflows that apply consistently across countries and waves with minimal extra effort.


A natural starting point is to combine the base function summary() with the familiar purrr::map() function to get an initial sense of a variable’s scale and distribution.






Tip



Always make sure the data is at the appropriate level for the variable being analysed. For instance, running summary statistics for disposable household income (dhi), defined at the household-level, from an individual-level dataset will silently duplicate observations, inflating counts and distorting distributional measures.



library(lissyrtools)
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)

it_data = lissyuse(data = 'it', vars = 'dhi', from = 2005)

it_data %>% purrr::map(~ summary(.x$dhi))

Beyond summary statistics, it is often useful to build small helper functions that capture a specific aspect of a variable and then apply them systematically across all available datasets. This approach keeps the workflow modular and easy to extend.
As a practical illustration, consider measuring data coverage: for a given income component, what share of observations are both non-missing and non-zero? This is especially relevant for variables like capital income (hicapital), which may be consistently recorded in some country-years but sparse or absent in others.

it_data = lissyuse(data = 'it', vars = c('dhi', 'hicapital'), from = 2005)

share_non_missing_non_zero <- function(df, variable_of_interest) {

    denominator = nrow(df)
    numerator   = sum( (!is.na(df[variable_of_interest])) & (df[variable_of_interest] !=0) )
    numerator_zero = sum((df[variable_of_interest] == 0)) 

    share_to_out = ( (numerator) / denominator ) * 100
    return(share_to_out)
}

title: Describing Data
text:
Beyond summary statistics, it is often useful to build small helper functions that capture a specific aspect of a variable and then apply them systematically across all available datasets. This approach keeps the workflow modular and easy to extend.
As a practical illustration, consider measuring data coverage: for a given income component, what share of observations are both non-missing and non-zero? This is especially relevant for variables like capital income (hicapital), which may be consistently recorded in some country-years but sparse or absent in others.

it_data = lissyuse(data = 'it', vars = c('dhi', 'hicapital'), from = 2005)

share_non_missing_non_zero <- function(df, variable_of_interest) {

    denominator = nrow(df)
    numerator   = sum( (!is.na(df[variable_of_interest])) & (df[variable_of_interest] !=0) )
    numerator_zero = sum((df[variable_of_interest] == 0)) 

    share_to_out = ( (numerator) / denominator ) * 100
    return(share_to_out)
}

purrr::map(it_data, ~ share_non_missing_non_zero(.x, 'hicapital'))

title: Describing Data
text:
We close with an important note on how percentiles are estimated, as the choice of method directly affects the comparability of results with LIS official figures.
LIS adopts Definition 4 from Hyndman and Fan (1996) for the computation of all percentile-based estimates, including medians, percentile ratios, poverty lines, and decile shares. Full details are available in this LIS methodological note.
The function run_weighted_percentiles() follows this methodology by default, so users can rely on it to produce estimates that are fully consistent with LIS standards without needing to configure anything manually.


spain_data <- lissyuse(data = "es", vars = "dhi", from = 2020)

run_weighted_percentiles(spain_data, var_name = 'dhi', probs = 0.5)

title: FAQs
text:
Can I download the LIS/LWS data?
No. Due to data confidentiality measures, the LIS microdata cannot be downloaded.
What statistical packages can I use with LISSY?
R (4.4.2), SAS (9.4), SPSS (22), and Stata (19.0) all work with LISSY.
May I use external files with the LIS databases?
If you wish to use external files with the microdata, send your request along with the attached file to usersupport@lisdatacenter.org. Your request will be reviewed and, if it meets security standards, you will receive an email with instructions on how to access your file.

What are the forbidden words?

The forbidden words depend on the statistical package used. LISSY automatically applies pre- and post-processing checks to ensure data confidentiality is never breached. Some syntax and commands may trigger security alerts — for example, syntax that displays frequencies on continuous variables or that would allow users to print individual records.
Do not include the following commands in your job:

SAS: print, NOXWAIT, NOXSYNC
SPSS: print
Stata: list, erase, rm, pwd, cd, rmdir, type, dir, ls

What does “set for review” mean, and how can I avoid this?
When LISSY detects a potentially suspicious job, it moves it to a security area for manual review and returns the error message set for review. To avoid this, adjust your code to avoid any syntax that could allow printing variables, regardless of programming language. Note that manually reviewed jobs may take some time to process — avoid resubmitting the same job until it has been handled.
What does “handling listing” or “job has been automatically killed” mean, and how can I avoid this?
The most common cause is an excessively long listing. To avoid this:

Split your program code into smaller parts and send several shorter job submissions.
Limit the number of datasets combined in a single run as much as possible.
Include commands in your code to shorten outputs, such as:

SAS: OPTIONS nosource nonotes
Stata: nolog, quietly, or noisily


I get an error message in my output. Is there a way to debug my program?
Debugging can be helped by testing your code on your own computer using the LIS or LWS downloadable sample files before submitting to LISSY. Note that no conclusions should be drawn from these artificial samples — they are created for instructional and debugging purposes only.
Can I receive non-ASCII output from LISSY (e.g. worksheets, HTML pages)?
Not currently. LISSY only returns plain ASCII output/listings from SAS, SPSS, R, and Stata.
Why do I receive the error “Could not connect to the server”?
This occurs when LISSY is temporarily down. Feel free to contact usersupport@lisdatacenter.org if you encounter this problem.

title: FAQs
text:
Replications with Revised Data

Data Archiving System in LISSY
Applies only to datasets revised after May/June 2019, and for journal review purposes only.
Following the 2019 LIS Template release, LIS introduced a data archiving system to support replication of analyses on datasets that have since been revised. This tool is intended exclusively for peer review activities or researchers needing to replicate published results, and access is granted for a maximum of two weeks.


How to request access to an earlier version of a revised dataset?
Write to LIS user support at usersupport@lisdatacenter.org specifying:

The database (LIS or LWS)
The statistical package used (Stata, R, SAS, or SPSS)
The date on which you accessed the dataset(s) and ran your analysis

You will then receive an email with instructions on how to access the pre-revised datasets.
For users needing access to databases following the 2011 Template (i.e. the last version of datasets on LISSY prior to May 2019 for LIS and mid-June 2019 for LWS), select the project LISPRE from LISSY for the LIS Database, and LWSPRE for the LWS Database.

title: Best Practises
text:
Before submitting a job to LISSY, we recommend using the sample files to prototype and debug in advance the jobs locally.
Send each job only once. If it is not returned, do not send it again. Moreover, wait for each job to be returned before submitting your next one.
Try breaking statistical queries into several smaller jobs since queries that generate very large outputs can cause system congestion. Always select only the variables needed for the analysis, and when working with many country-year datasets, split the workload into multiple jobs whenever possible.
Do not attempt to view, examine, or print individual records at either the person or household level. In addition, certain program syntax and commands will trigger system security alerts and may interrupt traffic.
Do not use commands that violate our security measures. More on this in the FAQs.
Do not request frequencies on continuous variables, as this tends to violate our security measures.
If you are an R user always use the original names of LIS variables when calling lissyrtools such as: run_weighted_count(), or run_weighted_mean() , always use the original names of LIS variables (for example, var_name = 'own' rather than var_name = 'my_version_of_own'). See this section on original variable names for details.
To create multiple charts in a single job run, the user needs to name them differently. More on this topic in the following links for Stata and R.
R packages and Stata ado files can only be installed by the LIS Staff into the LISSY system. Please contact User Support if you wish to do so.

title: Submit your First Job
text:
The interface
Upon first logging into LISSY, users have access to an intuitive interface where they can write and run unlimited jobs using LIS data in their preferred coding language. The interface allows users to:

Write and run jobs in a dedicated code editor;
View the printed output of their jobs, as in Stata, RStudio, or VSCode;
Produce visualizations;
Download all outputs to their local machine;
Access their full archive of past jobs.

Job Session Pane
The first stage of using LISSY begins in the Edit Job pane, where users must configure two drop-down menus at the top of the editor:

Project - the database to work with (e.g. LIS, LWS, LCS, ERFLIS);
Package - the coding language for the job (R, Stata, SAS, or SPSS).

Users must also provide a Subject — a short title identifying the job.
Once all fields are defined, users can write or paste their script in the job editor below. When ready, the job can be submitted by pressing the green button with the white arrow in the top-left corner of the editor, as shown in the illustration below:










Tip



For a smoother experience, we strongly recommend using our Sample Files to prototype your jobs in the editor (Stata, RStudio, etc…) you are most comfortable with. Once your code is ready and locally tested with the sample data, you can simply copy and paste it into the platform and adjust it for the real LIS microdata.
Stata users can find and download the sample files here, while R users can directly install the lissyrtools package, which already includes them. This package will be introduced in more detail in the section dedicated to R users.


Once the job has been submitted, switch to the Recent Jobs pane, where the output of your submitted job will soon become available.




Here you can see that the interface is divided into a left-hand and a right-hand side. On the left-hand side, you will find the menu listing your jobs. At the top of this list, the most recent job appears with an ampersand icon, indicating that it is still being executed. On the right-hand side, you can view the code of the job currently selected from the menu on the left.
If needed, for example, if you notice a typo in the code or if the execution is taking too long, you can also abort the running job by pressing the red button indicated in the image above.
Once the job has completed successfully, the ampersand icon will be replaced by a green check mark. This will be accompanied by the appearance of the listing pane, highlighted in blue. Clicking on it will display the printed output as well as any charts produced by the job (see the first image at the top of this page).




Finally, to download all generated materials directly to your local machine, simply click the disk icon, which gathers everything into a zipped folder and downloads it to your computer.
Job Archive Pane
In the top menu, between the Job Session pane and the logout button, you will find the Job Archive pane.
All jobs submitted through LISSY are archived and can be accessed here. You can search for previous jobs using several filters to refine your query according to different criteria. The system will then display all jobs matching your selected requirements in the menu on the left-hand side. You can open any archived job to review its code and outputs, as well as download all related materials directly to your local machine.

title: Submit your First Job
text:
Run the first job
Here and throughout the rest of this user guide, we provide code snippets that can be directly copied and pasted into LISSY, allowing for a hands-on approach to learning the topics covered in the following sections.
For Stata users, you can use the snippet below to begin exploring the interface on your own.

** Importing LIS microdata
lissyuse, iso2(se es) from(2018) to(2019) hvars(hid dhi dname iso2 year)

** Normal output
levelsof dname, local(levels)
foreach ccyy of local levels {
  di "`ccyy'"   
  sum dhi if dname == "`ccyy'"
}

** Comma-separated output
levelsof dname, local(levels)
local n = 0
foreach ccyy of local levels {
  local ++n
  qui sum dhi if dname == "`ccyy'"
  local mean_dhi : di %9.1f r(mean)
  if `n' == 1 {
          di "Dataset, Mean disposable income"
        }
        di "`ccyy', `mean_dhi'"
}

For R users, an equivalent example is provided below so that you can explore the interface using your preferred working environment.

library(lissyrtools)
library(dplyr)
data_list =  lissyrtools::lissyuse(
  data = c('es', 'se'), 
  vars = 'dhi', 
  from = 2018, 
  to = 2019, 
  database = 'lis'
)  

results = lissyrtools::run_weighted_mean(
  data = data_list,
  var_name = 'dhi'
)

print(results) 

# Tidying up into a tabular structure
lissyrtools::structure_to_plot( 
  results 
) %>% write.csv()

You may already notice a few distinctive features in the snippets above, particularly the Stata commands and R packages specifically designed for use within LISSY.
Apart from these LISSY-specific elements which will naturally be adressed later in in this guide, working in LISSY is very similar to using Stata or R in your usual workflow and working environment.

title: Submit your First Job
text:
Export Output
One especially important aspect of working in LISSY is learning how to structure and export your output properly, so that your results can be easily retrieved and reused afterward.
LISSY provides several ways to access and download your outputs:

All job outputs are automatically sent to your registered email address.
Outputs can also be downloaded directly from the interface by clicking the Disk icon.
Results are additionally available in PDF format for convenient viewing and sharing.
If your output is intended for tabular analysis, it is strongly recommended to export it in comma-separated values (CSV) format. This makes it easy to open the results directly in spreadsheet software or copy them into other applications for further analysis.

More detailed examples of exporting outputs in both R and Stata will be provided throughout the remainder of this user guide.

title: Describing Data
text:
Being able to describe newly imported data is a critical step, particularly in an environment where users cannot freely browse the underlying microdata.
This section introduces routine coding tasks designed to maximize descriptive insight on a variable with minimal code. These practices help users identify patterns and inconsistencies across datasets such as: breaks in a series, shifts in the level of disaggregation, the availability of non-zero and non-missing values for income variables across countries and years, etc…
In METIS, a substantial amount of descriptive information is already provided for each variable in a dataset, as illustrated in the figure below:
However, this information is currently displayed for one dataset (ccyy) at a time. To complement this, we will take a different approach: describing a single variable across countries series simultaneously, already taking advantage of the fact that the data are stored as a list of multiple ccyy data frames.
Using purrr::map() together with appropriate helper functions, it becomes straightforward to apply the same descriptive routine across multiple datasets, while ensuring that the output is already structured by country-year.
In support of this workflow, lissyrtools provides three useful functions:
We begin with categorical variables and how to perform exploratory and frequency analysis on them, before moving on to continuous variables. In addition to standard summary statistics such as the mean and percentiles, we will also demonstrate how to define custom functions, for instance, to compute the share of non-missing observations.

title: Describing Data
text:
Standardized variables
One-way tabulation
To quickly get a first look at a variable’s categories and how the sample is distributed across them, we can perform a straightforward one-way tabulation returning absolute frequencies for each category:

library(lissyrtools)
library(dplyr)

imported_list <- lissyuse(
  data = c('mx', 'es'), 
  vars = 'sex', 
  from = 2020
  )

lissyrtools::run_weighted_count(
    data = imported_list, 
    var_name = 'sex', 
    wgt_name = NULL, 
    percent = FALSE, 
    na.rm = FALSE
    )

The function run_weighted_count() takes a list of LIS/LWS/LCS datasets as its data argument and returns a tabulation of the variable specified in var_name.






Tip



Because the output is itself a list: one element per country-year, it can be piped directly into purrr::map() for further operations for each ccyy.


Now that we have a clear picture of the absolute counts, it is straightforward to switch to relative frequencies by setting percent = TRUE:

lissyrtools::run_weighted_count(
    data = imported_list, 
    var_name = 'sex', 
    wgt_name = NULL, 
    percent = TRUE,  
    na.rm = FALSE

The unweighted shares above reflect the sample composition. To obtain population-representative shares, we can pass a weight variable via wgt_name.






Note



Weight variables are always imported by default. There is no need to include them explicitly in lissyuse. To check the names of the columsn in the data frames run: print(names(imported_list[[1]]))



lissyrtools::run_weighted_count(
    data = imported_list, 
    var_name = 'sex', 
    wgt_name = 'ppopwgt',

Two-way tabulation
Datasets sometimes contain pairs of categorical variables where one is a finer disaggregation of the other. The variables educ and educlev are a prime example: educlev breaks each broad education category into more granular sub-groups. In such cases, a two-way tabulation serves a dual purpose. It describes the joint distribution of both variables simultaneously, and allows the user to verify which sub-categories of educlev correspond to which parent categories of educ.
run_weighted_count() supports this directly via the by argument. Always place the more disaggregated variable in var_name and the broader grouping variable in by:

imported_list <- lissyrtools::lissyuse(c('es18', 'mx18'), vars = c('educ', 'educlev'))

lissyrtools::run_weighted_count(imported_list, 'educlev', by = 'educ')

Nested coding
While standardized variables share a fixed category template across all datasets, this does not always guarantee straightforward comparability in practice. The level of detail available for a given variable can vary considerably across years within the same country series, reflecting differences in the underlying survey instrument. The variable own in the Spanish series illustrates this well.

lissyrtools::lissyuse(
  data = 'es', 
  vars = 'own', 
  from = 1999, 
  to = 2005
) %>% lissyrtools::run_weighted_count( var_name = 'own', wgt_name = NULL, percent = FALSE, na.rm = FALSE)  

 
$es05h
                    [100]owned            [110]owned outright 
                            18                           6892 
      [120]owned with mortgage    [211]rented at market price 
                          3187                            890 
[212]rented below market price              [220]free housing 
                           365                            853 

$es04h
                    [100]owned            [110]owned outright 
                            19                           7478 
      [120]owned with mortgage    [211]rented at market price 
                          3327                            886 
[212]rented below market price              [220]free housing
