$es00h
       [100]owned       [210]rented [220]free housing              <NA> 
             4204               487               274                 1 

$es99h
       [100]owned       [210]rented [220]free housing              <NA> 
             4352               493               283                 4 





In es00, housing tenure is recorded in three broad categories only, with all ownership grouped under a single code [100].

By es04, the same variable is captured with considerably more granularity, distinguishing for instance between outright ownership [110] and ownership with a mortgage [120], and similarly splitting the rental category into market [211] and sub-market [212] rentals.

This finer disaggregation in later years is not incidental: it reflects the hierarchical coding structure deliberately built into LIS/LWS/LCS standardized variables, where higher-level codes such as [100] or [200] represent aggregate categories, and lower-level codes such as [110], [120], or [211] represent their constituent sub-groups. Users should therefore always inspect the distribution of standardized categorical variables across the full country series before drawing comparisons, as apparent changes over time may reflect a shift in granularity rather than a genuine change in the underlying phenomenon.

title: Describing Data
text:
Country-specific variables
As the name suggests, country-specific variables are not designed to be comparable across countries. What is less immediately obvious is that they can also be unreliable for within-country comparisons over time: the categories used to capture a given concept may change from one wave to the next, either because the underlying survey instrument was revised or because the national classification itself evolved.
The variable ethnic_c in the United Kingdom series is a good illustration of how complex such variables can be in practice. The number of distinct ethnicity categories recorded has changed across waves, making any naive time-series comparison misleading without first understanding where those breaks occur.

lissyrtools::lissyuse(
  data = 'es', 
  vars = 'own', 
  from = 1999, 
  to = 2005
) %>% lissyrtools::run_weighted_count( var_name = 'own', wgt_name = NULL, percent = FALSE, na.rm = FALSE)

To assist with this, lissyrtools provides the variable_country_specific_categories() function, which prints the categories of a country-specific variable across all available waves for a given country. Setting the argument n_categories = TRUE returns only the count of distinct categories per wave rather than the full listing — a quick way to spot where breaks are likely occurring before committing to a deeper investigation,

lissyrtools::variable_country_specific_categories(
  variable = 'ethnic_c', 
  iso2 = 'uk',
  n_categories = TRUE
)

Important



For any substantive analysis involving country-specific variables, always load and inspect one country at a time. The same numerical code may carry an entirely different meaning depending on the country and wave, and mixing datasets without accounting for this will produce results that are difficult or impossible to interpret correctly.

title: Data Handling
text:
Once data has been successfully imported and explored, the next step is preparation for analysis. This stage bridges raw information and meaningful results by aligning the dataset with the specific requirements of the research design. Although the exact procedures depend on the research question, countries involved, subpopulations of interest, and empirical methods, common tasks typically include transforming variables to improve comparability, subsetting data to focus on relevant groups, and constructing new variables from existing ones.
Developing familiarity with these operations is essential, as they allow researchers to adapt datasets to their analytical goals while maintaining clarity and consistency. A structured approach to data manipulation also enhances workflow efficiency and reduces the risk of errors or misinterpretation during analysis.
As in the previous section, this part of the guide is organised by variable type, distinguishing between categorical and continuous data. By the end of this section, users will be equipped with a set of practical tools and techniques that add an additional layer of flexibility to their work with LIS data, ultimately expanding the range and depth of analyses they can perform.

title: Data Handling
text:
Highest-Level Recoding
To restore comparability across the full Spanish series, the more disaggregated categories available from 2004 onwards need to be collapsed back to the broader codes present at the start of the series, a process known as highest-level recoding.

library(lissyrtools)
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)
library(labelled)

recoded_data = lissyuse('es', 'own', from =  2000, to = 2004, database = 'lis') %>%
  purrr::map(
    ~ .x %>% mutate(
      own_copy_old  = own, # create a copy of the original variable 'own' 
      own = case_when( # do the transformations on the variable with the original name from LIS
        own >= 100 & own < 199 ~ 100, 
        own >= 210 & own < 219 ~ 210, 
        own >= 220 & own < 229 ~ 220, 
      ),
      own = haven::labelled(own, labels = labelled::val_labels(own_copy_old))
    ) 
  )

lissyrtools::run_weighted_count(data = recoded_data, var_name = 'own', na.rm = TRUE)

 
$es04h
       [100]owned       [210]rented [220]free housing 
            10824              1312               860 

$es00h
       [100]owned       [210]rented [220]free housing 
             4204               487               274 








Important



Functions in lissyrtools, only accept columns named after the original LIS, LWS and LCS variable names. Always perform recoding on the original variable directly, preserving a copy beforehand if needed. Variable names such as own_recoded or own_new will not be accepted — the variable must retain its original name (own, educ, educlev, and so on).




Spain — tenure variable own before recoding



Spain — tenure variable own after recoding

The two charts above illustrate the practical consequence of the nested coding structure and the value of the recoding step. In the first chart, the series breaks sharply around 2004, with the broad ownership category effectively disappearing as it splinters into finer subcategories introduced in later waves. A user working with the raw codes would face an artificial discontinuity that makes any longitudinal comparison across the full Spanish series unreliable. The second chart shows the result after recoding: by collapsing the more disaggregated categories back to the three broad codes present at the start of the series, the distribution becomes consistent across all waves and the series can be read and compared as intended.

title: Data Handling
text:
Due to the wide range of research questions that can be explored using data from LIS, it is often necessary to perform multiple and distinct types of data preparation after the initial import. For this reason, this section is divided into two parts, each dedicated to a different analytical goal.
In the first part, we demonstrate how to compute a Children Poverty Rate among Single-Mother Families. This particular indicator requires several steps, making it a comprehensive example of the types of functions users can rely on, as well as highlighting important considerations when working with LIS/LWS/LCS data.
In the second part, we focus on how to apply the deflators provided by LIS, an essential step for cross-country and cross-time comparisons, and discuss the specific nuances involved in that process.


The sections that follow illustrate a more comprehensive workflow, combining several preparation steps to construct a policy-relevant indicator from microdata.
The aim will be to compute the poverty rate among children in single-mother households in several countries. Constructing this indicator requires combining information available at both the household level (dhi, nhhmem17, hpartner), and the individual level (sex).






Important



Recall from the earlier sections of this guidebook when we introduced lissyuse(), that when both household and individual level variables are specified in vars, both files for a given ccyy are loaded and merged automatically. As a result, the data is loaded at the individual level.



library(lissyrtools)
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)

data <- lissyuse(
  data = c("us", "de", "uk", "fr"),  
  vars = c("dhi", "nhhmem17", "sex", "hpartner"), # 3 'h-level' + 1 'p-level'
  from = 2018, 
  to = 2024   
)  

The list contains the following `person-level` data frames: fr22, fr21, fr20, fr19, fr18, de22, de21, de20, de19, de18, uk24, uk23, uk22, uk21, uk20, uk19, uk18, us24, us23, us22, us21, us20, us19, us18.



columns = names(data[[1]]) 
lissyrtools::variable_labels(vars = columns)

                                             hid 
                          "household identifier" 
                                             dhi 
        "disposable household income, household" 
                                           dname 
                       "country/year identifier" 
                                            iso2 
                 "2-letter country abbreviation" 
                                            year 
                                "reference year" 
                                        currency 
                                "currency units" 
                                          nhhmem 
                   "number of household members" 
                                        nhhmem17 
     "number of household members 17 or younger" 
                                        hpartner 
"household reference person living with partner" 
                                            hwgt 
                   "normalised household weight" 
                                         hpopwgt 
                              "household weight" 
                                           hwgta 
                   "additional household weight" 
                                             pid 
                             "person identifier" 
                                             sex 
                                        "gender" 
                                        relation 
    "relationship to household reference person" 
                                            pwgt 
                      "normalised person weight" 
                                         ppopwgt 
                                 "person weight" 
                                           pwgta 
                      "additional person weight" 








Note



Variables relation and nhhmem are part of the group of variables that are always imported by default.




At this stage, we prepare the dataset so that it is aligned with the unit of analysis required for our indicator: the household. Although we imported both household- and person-level variables, the poverty measure is computed at the household level and then attributed to individuals (in this case, children).
We define a pipeline inside purrr::map() to apply the same sequence of transformations to each dataset. We begin by retaining only records corresponding to the household reference person (relation == 1000), ensuring that each household appears exactly once in the dataset and avoiding the duplication that would arise from keeping all person-level records. We then filter out observations with missing disposable household income (dhi), as these cannot contribute to the poverty calculation.

data_prep <- data %>%
  purrr::map(~ .x %>% 
        filter(relation == 1000) %>% 
        filter(!is.na(dhi)) %>% 
        mutate(
          new_wgt = hwgt * nhhmem,
          new_chld_wgt = hwgt * nhhmem17,
        )
  )

We then construct adjusted weights. For population-level indicators, we use a person-level weight derived from the household weight multiplied by household size (hwgt * nhhmem). For child-specific indicators, we instead construct a child weight by multiplying the household weight by the number of children in the household (hwgt * nhhmem17). These weights ensure that estimates correctly reflect the underlying population structure.


Before proceeding with inequality and poverty calculations, we address the presence of extreme income values. While the underlying microdata do not impose bounds on income, very high or very low values can disproportionately influence distributional measures.
To mitigate this, we apply bottom- and top-coding to disposable household income (dhi), with the help of an auxilliary function named apply_iqr_top_bottom_coding() tailored specifically for this step.

data_tb_coded <- data_prep %>%
    lissyrtools::apply_iqr_top_bottom_coding(
        var_name = 'dhi', 
        wgt_name = 'hwgt', 
        times = 3, 
        one_sided = NULL,
        type = 'type_4' 
        )

This adjustment is carried out on the logarithmic scale using an interquartile range (IQR) rule: values above the upper threshold (Q3 + 3×IQR) are capped, and values below the lower threshold (Q1 − 3×IQR) are raised. This method ensures that extreme observations do not disproportionately affect the results, while preserving the overall shape and structure of the income distribution.






Note



To ensure consistency with the methodology applied by LIS across all disseminated aggregate figures, this step must be performed prior to equivalisation. In addition, the quartiles used to define the IQR thresholds should be estimated following Definition 4 as proposed by Hyndman and Fan (1996), which corresponds to the type = "type_4" argument above





Households differ in size and composition, which affects their economic needs. To enable meaningful comparisons across households, we equivalize disposable household income.
We apply the square root equivalence scale, dividing household income by the square root of the total number of household members. This transformation accounts for economies of scale in consumption: larger households require more resources, but not proportionally more per additional member.
As a result, all individuals within a household are assigned the same equivalised income, regardless of their age or role within the household.

data_eqv <- data_tb_coded %>%
     lissyrtools::apply_sqrt_equivalisation(
        var_name = 'dhi'
        )



Having adjusted the income variable and reduced the dataset to the household level, we are now ready to compute the poverty line. We define it as 50% of the weighted median of equivalised income, which is the standard relative poverty threshold used in cross-national research.
We can use the already familiar run_weighted_percentiles(), which by default computes the minimum, maximum, and the 25th, 50th, and 75th percentiles, returning them as a named vector inside a list. The call below previews the output structure for the first dataset.

lissyrtools::run_weighted_percentiles(
        data_eqv[1], 
        var_name = "dhi", 
        wgt_name = "new_wgt"
    )

$fr22
         0%         25%         50%         75%        100% 
   665.9859  18918.6613  26299.4284  35709.9998 702890.3141 





We then use purrr::map() to apply this function across all datasets, retrieve the element corresponding to the median (named "50%"), and multiply it by 0.5 to establish the poverty line. This relative definition ensures that poverty is assessed in relation to the living standards prevailing within each dataset, so there is no need to adjust for inflation or different currencies.

medians <- purrr::map(
    lissyrtools::run_weighted_percentiles(
        data_eqv, 
        var_name = "dhi", 
        wgt_name = "new_wgt"
    ), "50%"
)
poverty_lines <- purrr::map(medians  , ~ .x  * 0.5)

print(poverty_lines)

It is important to note that the poverty line is always calculated based on the full population. This same threshold is subsequently applied when evaluating poverty rates for specific subgroups, such as children in single-mother households.


With the poverty line established, we create an indicator identifying whether each household falls below this threshold. For each observation, we compare equivalised income (dhi) to the poverty line.
Households with income below the threshold are classified as poor and assigned a value of 100, all others are assigned 0.

data_with_pov_line <- purrr::map2(
  data_eqv,
  poverty_lines,
  ~ .x %>%
    dplyr::mutate(
      line = .y,
      poor = dplyr::if_else(dhi < line, 100, 0)
    )
)







Tip



When using purrr::map2(), .x refers to the current element of the first list (data_eqv), while .y refers to the corresponding element of the second list (poverty_lines). This allows both lists to be iterated over in lockstep.




In the final step, we restrict the sample to the population of interest: children living in single-mother households. This is defined as households where the reference person is female (sex == 2), has no partner present (hpartner == 0), and where at least one child is present (nhhmem17 > 0).
We then compute the weighted mean of the poverty indicator using the child-specific weight (hwgt * nhhmem17 = new_chld_wgt). This produces the poverty rate among children in single-mother households, expressed as a percentage.
Throughout this process, the poverty line remains fixed, having been calculated for the total population, while the weighting scheme ensures that the estimate accurately reflects the distribution of children across households.

data_with_pov_line %>% 
  purrr::map( ~ .x %>%
         filter(hpartner==0 & sex==2 & nhhmem17>0)
  ) %>% 
  run_weighted_mean("poor", "new_chld_wgt")

title: Data Handling
text:
The sections that follow illustrate a more comprehensive workflow, combining several preparation steps to construct a policy-relevant indicator from microdata.
The aim will be to compute the poverty rate among children in single-mother households in several countries. Constructing this indicator requires combining information available at both the household level (dhi, nhhmem17, hpartner), and the individual level (sex).






Important



Recall from the earlier sections of this guidebook when we introduced lissyuse(), that when both household and individual level variables are specified in vars, both files for a given ccyy are loaded and merged automatically. As a result, the data is loaded at the individual level.



library(lissyrtools)
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)

data <- lissyuse(
  data = c("us", "de", "uk", "fr"),  
  vars = c("dhi", "nhhmem17", "sex", "hpartner"), # 3 'h-level' + 1 'p-level'
  from = 2018, 
  to = 2024   
)  

The list contains the following `person-level` data frames: fr22, fr21, fr20, fr19, fr18, de22, de21, de20, de19, de18, uk24, uk23, uk22, uk21, uk20, uk19, uk18, us24, us23, us22, us21, us20, us19, us18.

Note



Variables relation and nhhmem are part of the group of variables that are always imported by default.

title: Data Handling
text:
At this stage, we prepare the dataset so that it is aligned with the unit of analysis required for our indicator: the household. Although we imported both household- and person-level variables, the poverty measure is computed at the household level and then attributed to individuals (in this case, children).
We define a pipeline inside purrr::map() to apply the same sequence of transformations to each dataset. We begin by retaining only records corresponding to the household reference person (relation == 1000), ensuring that each household appears exactly once in the dataset and avoiding the duplication that would arise from keeping all person-level records. We then filter out observations with missing disposable household income (dhi), as these cannot contribute to the poverty calculation.

data_prep <- data %>%
  purrr::map(~ .x %>% 
        filter(relation == 1000) %>% 
        filter(!is.na(dhi)) %>% 
        mutate(
          new_wgt = hwgt * nhhmem,
          new_chld_wgt = hwgt * nhhmem17,
        )
  )

We then construct adjusted weights. For population-level indicators, we use a person-level weight derived from the household weight multiplied by household size (hwgt * nhhmem). For child-specific indicators, we instead construct a child weight by multiplying the household weight by the number of children in the household (hwgt * nhhmem17). These weights ensure that estimates correctly reflect the underlying population structure.

title: Data Handling
text:
Before proceeding with inequality and poverty calculations, we address the presence of extreme income values. While the underlying microdata do not impose bounds on income, very high or very low values can disproportionately influence distributional measures.
To mitigate this, we apply bottom- and top-coding to disposable household income (dhi), with the help of an auxilliary function named apply_iqr_top_bottom_coding() tailored specifically for this step.

data_tb_coded <- data_prep %>%
    lissyrtools::apply_iqr_top_bottom_coding(
        var_name = 'dhi', 
        wgt_name = 'hwgt', 
        times = 3, 
        one_sided = NULL,
        type = 'type_4' 
        )

This adjustment is carried out on the logarithmic scale using an interquartile range (IQR) rule: values above the upper threshold (Q3 + 3×IQR) are capped, and values below the lower threshold (Q1 − 3×IQR) are raised. This method ensures that extreme observations do not disproportionately affect the results, while preserving the overall shape and structure of the income distribution.






Note



To ensure consistency with the methodology applied by LIS across all disseminated aggregate figures, this step must be performed prior to equivalisation. In addition, the quartiles used to define the IQR thresholds should be estimated following Definition 4 as proposed by Hyndman and Fan (1996), which corresponds to the type = "type_4" argument above

title: Data Handling
text:
Households differ in size and composition, which affects their economic needs. To enable meaningful comparisons across households, we equivalize disposable household income.
We apply the square root equivalence scale, dividing household income by the square root of the total number of household members. This transformation accounts for economies of scale in consumption: larger households require more resources, but not proportionally more per additional member.
As a result, all individuals within a household are assigned the same equivalised income, regardless of their age or role within the household.

data_eqv <- data_tb_coded %>%
     lissyrtools::apply_sqrt_equivalisation(
        var_name = 'dhi'
        )

title: Data Handling
text:
Having adjusted the income variable and reduced the dataset to the household level, we are now ready to compute the poverty line. We define it as 50% of the weighted median of equivalised income, which is the standard relative poverty threshold used in cross-national research.
We can use the already familiar run_weighted_percentiles(), which by default computes the minimum, maximum, and the 25th, 50th, and 75th percentiles, returning them as a named vector inside a list. The call below previews the output structure for the first dataset.

lissyrtools::run_weighted_percentiles(
        data_eqv[1], 
        var_name = "dhi", 
        wgt_name = "new_wgt"
    )

$fr22
         0%         25%         50%         75%        100% 
   665.9859  18918.6613  26299.4284  35709.9998 702890.3141 





We then use purrr::map() to apply this function across all datasets, retrieve the element corresponding to the median (named "50%"), and multiply it by 0.5 to establish the poverty line. This relative definition ensures that poverty is assessed in relation to the living standards prevailing within each dataset, so there is no need to adjust for inflation or different currencies.

medians <- purrr::map(
    lissyrtools::run_weighted_percentiles(
        data_eqv, 
        var_name = "dhi", 
        wgt_name = "new_wgt"
    ), "50%"
)
poverty_lines <- purrr::map(medians  , ~ .x  * 0.5)

print(poverty_lines)

title: R Users
text:
Welcome R people 👋

What you’ll find here
This guide walks you step by step through working with LIS data in R — from getting started to building a solid, reproducible workflow.
You’ll learn how to navigate the structure and specific features of LIS datasets, while developing practical skills you can apply directly to your own projects. We cover each stage of the workflow, highlight common operations, and share tips to help you work more efficiently.
Most examples rely on the in-house R package lissyrtools, designed to simplify and streamline your interaction with LIS data.
Whether you’re new to LIS or looking to improve your workflow, this guide aims to provide a clear and hands-on learning experience.
If you have any questions or feedback, feel free to contact the LIS team.


Additional Resources

The R package lissyrtools

Self-Teaching Resources

title: Import Data
text:
More than a thousand LIS, LWS and LCS datasets are available for use and analysis within LISSY. Learning how to import these datasets is one of the first key steps in the user workflow, as it requires becoming familiar with the built-in tools specifically designed for this purpose.
Before getting started, there are a few important concepts to keep in mind:
R users have two different methods available to import data into LISSY:
For the remainder of this guide, we will focus on Method 1, which imports the selected LIS datasets into a list, where each element corresponds to a specific country–year dataset.

title: Import Data
text:
Advantage 1: Import entire country series
At the time we are writting this guide, LIS contains 26 datasets on Italy. This means that if the user wanted to import all years it would have needed to manually specify 26 distinct datasets. On top of it, it still had to know and confirm the exact specific years that we have data for each one of the countries.

* it22 it20 it16 it14 it12 ...

To bypass this problem, lissyuse() allows users to import LIS data by specifying the countries they wish to work with via their ISO-2 country codes, as well as optionally filtering by a desired year range.

lis_data <- lissyrtools::lissyuse(
  data = c('it'), 
  vars = "dhi"
)

The list contains the following `household-level` data frames: it22h, it20h, it16h, it14h, it12h, it10h, it08h, it06h, it04h, it02h, it00h, it98h, it95h, it93h, it91h, it89h, it87h, it86h, it84h, it83h, it82h, it81h, it80h, it79h, it78h, it77h.

class(lis_data)
names(lis_data)
class(lis_data[[1]])

 
[1] "list"
 [1] "it22h" "it20h" "it16h" "it14h" "it12h" "it10h" "it08h" "it06h" "it04h"
[10] "it02h" "it00h" "it98h" "it95h" "it93h" "it91h" "it89h" "it87h" "it86h"
[19] "it84h" "it83h" "it82h" "it81h" "it80h" "it79h" "it78h" "it77h"
[1] "tbl_df"     "tbl"        "data.frame"








Important



The output of lissyrtools::lissyuse() will always be a list of data frames. Each ccyy is a different data frame.


To filter the datasets to a shorter time span, the user can also specify the from and to arguments.

lis_data <- lissyrtools::lissyuse(
  data = c("mx", "us"), 
  vars = "dhi",
  from = 2014,
  to = 2016
)

The list contains the following `household-level` data frames: mx16h, mx14h, us16h, us15h, us14h.


Specific datasets can also be selected by specifying its ccyy code

lis_data <- lissyrtools::lissyuse(
  data = c("it16", "mx", "us"), 
  vars = "dhi",
  from = 2014,
  to = 2016
)

The list contains the following `household-level` data frames: it16h, mx16h, mx14h, us16h, us15h, us14h.

title: Import Data
text:
Advantage 2: Automatic Data-Level Selection
The second benefit of using lissyuse() is that it automatically imports datasets at the level determined by the variables selected. If the users selects only household-level varaibles in the vars argument such as: disposable household income (dhi), geographic region (region_c) or capital income (hicapital), the data will be loadad at the household level. As soon as the user includes an individual-level variable, such as gender (sex) or labour force status (lfs), the dataset level adjusts accordingly.
To help users identify the imported data level, a message is printed each time lissyuse() is executed. In addition, the names of the datasets include an h suffix when household-level data is loaded.

h_level_data <- lissyrtools::lissyuse(
  data = "lu18", 
  vars = c("dhi", "region_c", "typehh") # only h-level 
)

The list contains the following `household-level` data frames: lu18h.


In the example below, only individual-level variables are specified. In such cases, in addition to the printed message indicating the data level, the names of the data frames will contain a p suffix.

p_level_data <- lissyrtools::lissyuse(
  data = "lu18", 
  vars = c("age", "sex", "relation", "emp", "pi11")
)

The list contains the following `person-level` data frames: lu18p.


If both household-level and individual-level variables are specified in vars, no suffix is added to the name of the data frame.

merged_hhd_ind_data <- lissyrtools::lissyuse(
  data = "lu18", 
  vars = c("dhi", "region_c", "typehh", "age", "sex", "relation", "emp", "pi11")
)

The list contains the following `person-level` data frames: lu18.

names(merged_hhd_ind_data[[1]])

 
 [1] "hid"      "dhi"      "region_c" "dname"    "iso2"     "year"    
 [7] "currency" "nhhmem"   "typehh"   "hwgt"     "hpopwgt"  "hwgta"   
[13] "pid"      "pi11"     "emp"      "age"      "sex"      "relation"
[19] "pwgt"     "ppopwgt"  "pwgta"   








Important



Recap: As soon as an indiviudal-level variable is selected in the argument vars, the data will be loaded at individual-level as well. If only household-level variables are selected, then data will be loaded at household-level. If none are selected, then all variables are considered and consequently data will be at the individual-level.








Tip



Note as well that some variables were imported by default. Variables such as IDs, weights, and others do not need to be defined explicitly, as they are automatically included.

title: Import Data
text:
Importing LWS and LCS data
To import data from these databases, one would need to change the selection in the Project drop-down menu, and set the database argument equal to lws or lcs accordingly.





us_lws_data = lissyrtools::lissyuse(
  data = c("us"), 
  vars = c("dnw"), # disposable net wealth - LWS specific variable. 
  from = 2015, 
  database = 'lws' 
)

The list contains the following `household-level` data frames: us22h, us19h, us16h.

be_lcs_data = lissyrtools::lissyuse(
  data = c("be"), 
  vars = c("hc01_t"), # LCS specific variable. 
  from = 2018, 
  database = 'lcs' 
)

The list contains the following `household-level` data frames: be24h, be22h, be20h, be18h.

title: Structuring Results for Analysis
text:
Export to CSV
With the data now shaped into a clean tabular format, we can take the next step: exporting it for use outside LISSY. One convenient feature of the LISSY console is that it allows you to directly output your results in a format that can easily be transferred into spreadsheet software such as Excel.
We will now illustrate how to do this step by step. To do so, we construct a new example that goes through the full analytical workflow: importing the data, preparing the income variable, computing an aggregate measure, and finally restructuring the output into a tabular format.

library(lissyrtools)
library(tidyverse)
library(purrr)


mx_pe_datasets = lissyuse(
  data = c('mx', 'pe'), 
  vars = 'dhi', 
  from = 2010, 
  to = 2020
  ) 


output_df <-  mx_pe_datasets %>% 
  map(~ .x %>% 
        filter(!is.na(dhi)) %>% 
        mutate(new_wgt = nhhmem * hwgt)
  ) %>%
  apply_iqr_top_bottom_coding('dhi', 'hwgt') %>%
  apply_sqrt_equivalisation('dhi') %>% 
  run_weighted_gini('dhi', 'new_wgt') %>%
  structure_to_plot()  

With this done, we can now call the write.csv() function to print the data we have created directly into the LISSY console.

write.csv(output_df, row.names = FALSE)





Once the output appears in the console, you can transfer it into a spreadsheet as follows:

Use your mouse to select the entire output displayed in the LISSY console
Copy it using Ctrl + C (on Windows/Linux) or Cmd + C (on macOS)
Open a new spreadsheet in Excel (or similar software)
Paste the content into cell A1





If the data does not automatically split into columns, use the “Text to Columns” (or equivalent) feature and specify a comma as the delimiter. This will correctly separate the values into columns.




This approach provides a simple and effective way to export aggregate results from LISSY, where users are not allowed to directly download files to a local storage folder. Instead, LISSY allows the download of job-related outputs such as the submitted code, the corresponding listings, and any generated visualizations (typically in image format).
Even in cases where personal storage is available, all outputs are subject to a disclosure control process: results must be reviewed and approved by LIS staff before they can be released to the user.
Within this context, exporting data via the console offers a practical workaround. By formatting aggregate results as CSV and copying them into a spreadsheet, users can quickly transfer structured data into external tools for further analysis, formatting, or presentation, without bypassing the platform’s safeguards.

title: Structuring Results for Analysis
text:
So far, most of our outputs have been returned as lists. This is intentional, as direct printing of data frames is not possible in LISSY for security reasons.
Nevertheless, structuring results in a tabular format (rows × columns) ensures compatibility with standard data workflows, making it straightforward to integrate the results into downstream tasks such as visualization, or modelling.
In addition, a tabular structure makes the data easier to export, allowing users to continue further analysis, as well as to reuse and inspect the data more effectively.

title: Structuring Results for Analysis
text:
structure_to_plot()
The function structure_to_plot() was designed to convert complex outputs into a format suitable for analysis and visualization. Specifically, it transforms the results produced by the lissyrtools::run_weighted_*() family of functions, from nested lists, into tidy tabular data frames in long format.
To illustrate this, and to provide a visual representation of the resulting output, we present examples using lissyrtools locally with some of its embedded sample datasets. This approach reflects how a user would interact with lissyrtools outside of LISSY, working on their local machine, which is made possible through the inclusion of these embedded datasets.



library(lissyrtools)
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)

available_sample_datasets = c(
    'it14', 'it16', 'it20',
    'mx14', 'mx16', 'mx18',
    'us14', 'us16', 'us18'
)
datasets_final <- lissyuse(
  data = available_sample_datasets, 
  vars = c('educ', 'pilabour', 'age', 'emp', 'sex'), 
  from = 2014, 
  to = 2018, 
  database = 'lis'  
  ) 




output_as_list <- datasets_final %>% 
  purrr::map(~ .x %>% 
    filter(age>23 & age <56) %>% 
    filter(emp ==1)
  ) %>%
  apply_ppp_adjustment(var_name = 'pilabour', database = 'lis', transformation = 'lisppp', base_year_ppp = 2021) %>%
  run_weighted_mean('pilabour')

print(output_as_list)  

$Italy
    2014     2016     2020 
34901.71 40272.41 49846.01 

$Mexico
    2014     2016     2018 
8812.436 9331.102 8713.375 

$`United States`
    2014     2016     2018 
59617.25 63539.52 63173.74 


Now that we have the aggregate figures in a familiar format, we simply need to pass this object to the structure_to_plot() function to seamlessly restructure it into a tidy data frame, as depicted below:

lissyrtools::structure_to_plot(output_as_list)   





If the user performs a more disaggregated analysis that goes beyond a simple figure by country and year, by instead adding a subgroup layer through the by argument in some of the run_weighted_*() functions, structure_to_plot() also accommodates those cases automatically.

datasets_final %>% 
  map(~ .x %>% filter(age>23 & age <56) %>% filter(emp ==1)) %>%
  apply_ppp_adjustment(var_name = 'pilabour', database = 'lis', transformation = 'lisppp', base_year_ppp = 2021) %>% 
  run_weighted_mean('pilabour', by = 'educ') %>% 
  structure_to_plot()





Finally, it also goes a step further by accommodating figures for the indicator of interest across the distribution within a given subgroup for each country and year, making the process really user-friendly


datasets_final %>% 
  map(~ .x %>% filter(age>23 & age <56) %>% filter(emp ==1)) %>%
  apply_ppp_adjustment(var_name = 'pilabour', database = 'lis', transformation = 'lisppp', base_year_ppp = 2021) %>% 
  run_weighted_percentiles('pilabour', by = 'educ', average = TRUE) %>% 
  structure_to_plot()











Caution



Reminder that these examples are run locally using sample datasets, which are a subset of datasets available in LIS, specifically from countries where access to the microdata is publicly accessible.


With the data properly restructured into a tabular format, next we will show how to export it directly from the LISSY console into a CSV file, as well as how to plot it within LISSY.

title: Describing Data
text:
Being able to describe newly imported data is a critical step, particularly in an environment where users cannot freely browse the underlying microdata.
This section introduces routine coding tasks designed to maximize descriptive insight on a variable with minimal code. These practices help users identify patterns and inconsistencies across datasets such as: breaks in a series, shifts in the level of disaggregation, the availability of non-zero and non-missing values for income variables across countries and years, etc…
In METIS, a substantial amount of descriptive information is already provided for each variable in a dataset, as illustrated in the figure below:
However, this information is currently displayed for one dataset (ccyy) at a time. To complement it, this section takes a different approach: describing a single variable across countries series simultaneously, leveraging the fact that the data are stored in a single dataset comprising microdata for multiple country-year pairs.
To retrieve an aggregate figure for a given value of the column dname (dataset name) without looping across country-year pairs, two approaches are available:
While the first approach is simpler to write, essentially a single line of code, its output can become lengthy and hard to read when many datasets are in use. The collapse approach, though more code-intensive, structures the data in a way that is well-suited for producing plots or exporting results to a spreadsheet in CSV format. Both uses are covered in the section on Structuring Results for Analysis.

title: Describing Data
text:
Standardized variables
Because standardized variables follow a fixed category structure across all countries and years, users can import and tabulate them with confidence. This makes it straightforward to assess the composition of a variable and get a first look at how the sample is distributed across groups for any given country-year. The examples below focus on one-way tabulations, which display both absolute and relative frequencies directly in LISSY. Two approaches are demonstrated throughout: the by command and the collapse command.
One-way tabulation - by command

One-way tabulation - collapse command
The collapse command provides a more structured alternative for obtaining frequency distributions. Rather than displaying figures directly in the console, collapse restructures the data into an aggregated dataset. This transformation, from microdata to aggregated data, is particularly well suited for producing visualizations or for printing the dataset to the console as a delimited string, which can then be copied and pasted into a spreadsheet for further inspection.






Tip

qui lissyuse, iso2(mx es) from(2020) pvars(pid sex ppopwgt) hvars(hid dname cname year)

preserve

    gen n = 1
    collapse (sum) n, by(sex cname year dname)
    bysort dname: egen total = total(n)
    gen percent = n / total *100
    decode sex, gen(gender) 

    forvalues i = 1/`=_N' {
        if `i' == 1 {
        di "cname,year,gender,percent"
        } 
        di cname[`i'] ","  year[`i'] "," gender[`i'] "," percent[`i']   
    }

restore

Using preserve and restore is not needed in the example above, but allows you to print the intended aggregated dataset, while allowing you to continue to reuse the microdata in a single job submission.


A few implementation details are worth noting. First, an auxiliary variable n is created and set to 1 for every observation before collapsing. This is a common and convenient technique: since collapse aggregates by summing, each row contributes exactly one unit to the count, so the sum of n within a group directly gives the number of observations in that group. Second, a dataset-level total is computed using bysort dname: egen total = total(n), which allows the within-group percentages to be calculated relative to the correct denominator for each country-year pair. Finally, decode sex is used to convert the numeric codes of the sex variable into their corresponding string labels, storing them in a new variable gender. Without this step, the output would display numeric codes only, making it harder to read at a glance, particularly when sharing results or preparing them for a plot or export.

Rather than summing observations, collapse now sums the weights within each group, so that the resulting percentages reflect the share of the population — rather than the sample — falling into each category. This is generally the preferred approach for substantive analysis, as it accounts for differences in sampling design across countries and years. The preserve/restore wrapper, the bysort-based denominator, and the decode step all carry over unchanged from the non-weighted example.

Two-way tabulation
One-way tabulations describe how a sample is distributed across the categories of a single variable. Sometimes however, datasets contain pairs of categorical variables where one is a finer disaggregation of the other. The variables educ and educlev are a prime example, where educlev breaks down each broad education category into more granular sub-groups. In such cases, a two-way tabulation serves a dual purpose: it describes the joint distribution of both variables simultaneously, and it allows the user to verify which categories of one variable correspond to which categories of the other, confirming that no unexpected combinations appear across countries or years.
The example below cross-tabulates educ and educlev for Mexico and Spain, computing the share of each educlev sub-category within its parent educ group.

qui lissyuse, iso2(mx es) from(2018) to(2018) pvars(pid educ educlev ppopwgt) hvars(cname year dname)
preserve
drop if (missing(educ) | missing(educlev))
gen n = 1
collapse (sum) n, by(dname cname year educ educlev)
bysort dname educ: egen total = total(n)
gen percent = n / total * 100
decode educ, gen(education) 
decode educlev, gen(education_level) 
forvalues i = 1/`=_N' {
    if `i' == 1 {
        di "cname@year@education@education_level@percent"
    } 
    di cname[`i'] "@" year[`i'] "@" education[`i'] "@" education_level[`i'] "@" percent[`i']   
}
restore

Nested coding
While standardized variables share a fixed category template across all countries and years, this does not always guarantee straightforward comparability in practice. The level of detail available for a given variable can vary considerably across years within the same country series, reflecting differences in the underlying survey instrument. The variable own in the Spanish series illustrates this well.

qui lissyuse, iso2(es) from(1999) to(2005) hvars(cname year dname)

bysort dname: tabulate own, missing

-> dname = es00
variable own not found
r(111);

r(111);



In es00, housing tenure is recorded in three broad categories only, with all ownership grouped under a single code [100].

By es04, the same variable is captured with considerably more granularity, distinguishing for instance between outright ownership [110] and ownership with a mortgage [120], and similarly splitting the rental category into market [211] and sub-market [212] rentals.

This finer disaggregation in later years is not incidental: it reflects the hierarchical coding structure deliberately built into LIS/LWS/LCS standardized variables, where higher-level codes such as [100] or [200] represent aggregate categories, and lower-level codes such as [110], [120], or [211] represent their constituent sub-groups. Users should therefore always inspect the distribution of standardized categorical variables across the full country series before drawing comparisons, as apparent changes over time may reflect a shift in granularity rather than a genuine change in the underlying phenomenon.

title: Describing Data
text:
Country-specific variables
Country-specific variables require special attention in LISSY. Unlike standardized variables, designed to be comparable across countries and over time, country-specific variables reflect the original national classifications and coding schemes used in each survey. As a result, they should always be handled on a dataset-by-dataset basis.
The lissyuse command appends all selected ccyy datasets into a single large dataset. While this is convenient for harmonised variables, it creates technical issues for country-specific variables. The same numerical codes may carry entirely different meanings depending on the country and year, and when datasets are stacked together, Stata attempts to reconcile conflicting value labels — often silently overwriting some with others.
To illustrate this, consider loading Italian, Spanish, and German data together and including region_c among the selected variables:

Extra tools in R
An additional complication arises when working across multiple waves of the same country: classifications themselves may change from one year to the next, making longitudinal comparisons unreliable without prior investigation.
For R users, the lissyrtools package provides a dedicated function, variable_country_specific_categories(), which helps assess the number of distinct categories a country-specific variable takes across waves of a given series. This allows you to identify classification breaks before attempting any trend analysis. For details, see the corresponding R section.

title: Data Handling
text:
Once data has been successfully imported and explored, the next step is preparation for analysis. This stage bridges raw information and meaningful results by aligning the dataset with the specific requirements of the research design. Although the exact procedures depend on the research question, countries involved, subpopulations of interest, and empirical methods, common tasks typically include transforming variables to improve comparability, subsetting data to focus on relevant groups, and constructing new variables from existing ones.
Developing familiarity with these operations is essential, as they allow researchers to adapt datasets to their analytical goals while maintaining clarity and consistency. A structured approach to data manipulation also enhances workflow efficiency and reduces the risk of errors or misinterpretation during analysis.
As in the previous section, this part of the guide is organised by variable type, distinguishing between categorical and continuous data. By the end of this section, users will be equipped with a set of practical tools and techniques that add an additional layer of flexibility to their work with LIS data, ultimately expanding the range and depth of analyses they can perform.

title: Data Handling
text:
Highest-Level Recoding
To restore comparability across the full Spanish series, the more disaggregated categories available from 2004 onwards need to be collapsed back to the broader codes present at the start of the series. In Stata, this is handled directly with the recode command, which maps ranges of existing values to a new target code in a single readable line:

qui lissyuse, iso2(es) hvars(hid hpopwgt own cname year dname) from(2020)
recode own (100/199 = 100) (210/219 = 210) (220/229 = 220)

Spain — tenure variable own before recoding



Spain — tenure variable own after recoding

The two charts above illustrate the practical consequence of the nested coding structure and the value of the recoding step. In the first chart, the series breaks sharply around 2004, with the broad ownership category effectively disappearing as it splinters into finer subcategories introduced in later waves. A user working with the raw codes would face an artificial discontinuity that makes any longitudinal comparison across the full Spanish series unreliable. The second chart shows the result after recoding: by collapsing the more disaggregated categories back to the three broad codes present at the start of the series, the distribution becomes consistent across all waves and the series can be read and compared as intended.

title: Data Handling
text:
Currency and Price Level Adjustments
Income, wealth, and consumption data provided by LIS are expressed in national currencies at current prices for the income reference year. While this preserves the data in a form close to its original source, it also creates clear comparability issues across countries.
For clarity, the snippet below retrieves the unweighted average of disposable household income (dhi) for both the United States and Sweden in 2018.

qui lissyuse, cc(us18 se18) hvars(dhi dname cname year)
tabstat dhi, by(dname)

Summary for variables: dhi
Group variable: dname (country/year identifier)

 dname |      Mean
-------+----------
  se18 |  504749.2
  us18 |  73735.58
-------+----------
 Total |  106215.4
------------------



The figures reported above are not directly comparable. The large difference in magnitude, with Sweden appearing to have values more than five times higher than those of the United States, does not reflect real differences in income levels, but rather the fact that the data are expressed in different national currencies, implying the need for additional transformation steps.
To address this issue, LIS provides both CPI and PPP deflators for each country and year. These allow users to convert values into a common, comparable scale. In practice, this process involves merging the deflator data with the countries’ microdata, so that the relevant transformation can be applied to the flow variables.




As shown in the example above, we have 3 columns with conversion factors that the user can make use of. These are:

Consumer Price Index: needed to compare real amounts over time within countries;
Purchasing Power Parity: needed to compare real amounts across countries;
LISPPP: which combine CPI and PPP deflators and can be used to compare real amounts across countries and over time.

We can now redo the exercise above by making use of the deflators dataset, which allows us to convert and adjust the dhi variable into international US dollars.

qui lissyuse, cc(us18 se18) hvars(dhi dname cname year)

    qui merge m:1 cname year  using "$myincl/ppp_2021.dta" ,  keep(match)      
    replace  dhi =  dhi / ppp 

tabstat dhi, by(dname)

(5,563 real changes made)


Summary for variables: dhi
Group variable: dname (country/year identifier)

 dname |      Mean
-------+----------
  se18 |  55795.59
  us18 |  73735.58
-------+----------
 Total |  72383.68
------------------



The Swedish figure is now much closer to American one, as both are expressed in international US dollars at 2021 prices. This adjustment makes the values directly comparable and better reflects real income levels.






Warning



In some LWS datasets, wealth amounts and income amounts might differ in their reference year. The year of the dataset always corresponds to the wealth amounts reference year, but income amounts might have been expressed as the ones in the year before.


To conclude this section on adjusting data for differences in currency and price levels, we present two additional examples illustrating how CPI and LISPPP deflators can be used in practice.
We begin with a case where the analysis focuses on a single country. In such situations, users may wish to keep results expressed in the country’s national currency while adjusting for inflation over time. Applying the CPI deflator allows values to be converted into constant prices, ensuring that changes reflect real variation rather than shifts in the price level.

qui lissyuse, cc(us18 se18) hvars(dhi dname cname year)
tabstat dhi, by(dname)

    qui merge m:1 cname year  using "$myincl/ppp_2021.dta" ,  keep(match)   
    replace  dhi =  dhi / cpi * 100

tabstat dhi, by(dname)

Summary for variables: dhi
Group variable: dname (country/year identifier)

-------+----------

  us18 |  73735.58
-------+----------

------------------


(73,386 real changes made)


Summary for variables: dhi
Group variable: dname (country/year identifier)

-------+----------

-------+----------

------------------



Alternatively, users may be interested in making comparisons across countries and over time. In this context, relying solely on CPI adjustments is not sufficient, as values would still be expressed in different national currencies. This is where the LISPPP deflator becomes particularly useful. By combining both CPI and PPP adjustments, it converts values into a international US dollars at a given base year, thereby enabling meaningful cross-country comparisons in real terms.

qui lissyuse, cc(us18 se18) hvars(dhi dname cname year)
tabstat dhi, by(dname)

    qui merge m:1 cname year  using "$myincl/ppp_2021.dta" ,  keep(match)   
    replace  dhi =  dhi / lisppp

tabstat dhi, by(dname)

Together, these approaches highlight the importance of selecting the appropriate deflator depending on the analytical objective, whether the focus is on within-country trends or cross-country comparability.

title: Import Data
text:
More than a thousand LIS, LWS and LCS datasets are available for use and analysis within LISSY. Learning how to import these datasets is one of the first essential steps in the user workflow, as it requires becoming familiar with the built-in tools specifically designed for this purpose.
Before getting started, there are a few important concepts to keep in mind:
Stata users have two different methods available to import data into LISSY:
In this guide, we focus primarily on Method 1, based on the lissyuse command. This method imports the selected LIS datasets into a single appended dataset while simplifying dataset selection and file management.

title: Import Data
text:
Advantage 1: Importing Entire Country Series
As noted above, LIS data is stored separately for each country–year combination, identified by a ccyy code.
At the time of writing, LIS contains 28 datasets for Austria and 22 for Switzerland. Importing all available years manually would therefore require specifying 50 individual datasets. In addition, the user would need to know exactly which years are available for each country.

* at23 at22 at21 at20 at19 ...
* ch22 ch21 ch20 ch19 ch18 ...

To simplify this process, lissyuse allows users to specify only the countries they wish to work with through their ISO2 country codes, together with a desired time range using the from() and to() options:

In practice, this is usually inefficient. Therefore, users are strongly encouraged to specify variables explicitly using the hvars() and pvars() options.

title: Structuring Results for Analysis
text:
Throughout the previous chapters, we have highlighted the usefulness of collapse for transforming microdata into aggregated datasets by country-year and selected subpopulations. This is particularly valuable in an environment like LISSY, where direct inspection of the microdata is not possible, and users must rely on techniques that produce structured, exportable summaries.
With this in mind, this chapter closes the guidebook with two practical sections: the first walks through exporting aggregated results in a delimited format compatible with CSV, and the second introduces how to produce visualizations directly within the LISSY environment.
Export to CSV
To illustrate this process step by step, we start by coding country-level inequality figures for Mexico and Peru, covering the workflow stages addressed in previous chapters: importing, processing, and aggregating microdata.
Finally, we display the results using a comma-separated format, with columns for country name, year, and the inequality figure of interest.

    // 1) Load data 

qui lissyuse, iso2(mx pe) from(2010) to(2020) ///
          hvars(hid hwgt nhhmem dhi dname cname year) // (data is at household-level)


*==========================================
* Identify and loop over selected datasets
*=========================================
     
qui levelsof dname, local(levels)
local x : word 1 of `levels'

foreach ccyy of local levels {
        
    **
    preserve
    **
    qui {
    keep if dname == "`ccyy'"


        // 2) Data preparation 

    *===================================
    * Filter out missing observations 
    *===================================
     
    drop if missing(dhi)
     
    *===================================
    * Create person weight (data is at household-level)
    *===================================
     
    generate double pwt = hwgt * nhhmem 
     
    *===================================
    * Bottom and top coding / outlier detection
    *===================================

    generate double dhi_log = log(dhi) 
    replace dhi_log = 0 if dhi_log == . & dhi != . 

    sort dhi_log hwgt
    qui percentils dhi_log [aw = hwgt], p(25 75)
    local p75 = e(Perc_75)
    local p25 = e(Perc_25) 
    gen double iqr = `p75' - `p25' 
    gen double upper_bound = `p75'  + (iqr * 3)  
    gen double lower_bound = `p25'  - (iqr * 3)  
    replace dhi=exp(upper_bound) if dhi>exp(upper_bound)  
    replace dhi=exp(lower_bound) if dhi<exp(lower_bound)  

    *===================================
    * Equivalise income (square root)
    *===================================

    generate double ey = ( dhi / (nhhmem^0.5) )


        // 3) Compute Key Figures 

    *===================================
    * Gini Coefficient
    *===================================

    quietly sum ey [w = pwt] , de
    local cumsum_w = r(sum_w)
    local mean_ey = r(mean) 
    sort ey
    egen double gini = sum( (2 * sum(pwt) + 1 - pwt)  * pwt * (ey - `mean_ey') / (`cumsum_w'^2 * `mean_ey') )
    }

        if dname[1] == "`x'" {
        di "     "
        di "cname,year,indicator,value"
        } 
        dis cname[1], "," year[1], "," "Gini Coefficient" "," gini[1]
    

    **
    restore
    **
}

 24.     }
 25.

Once the output appears in the console, you can transfer it into a spreadsheet as follows:

Use your mouse to select the entire output displayed in the LISSY console
Copy it using Ctrl + C (on Windows/Linux) or Cmd + C (on macOS)
Open a new spreadsheet in Excel (or similar software)
Paste the content into cell A1





If the data does not automatically split into columns, use the “Text to Columns” (or equivalent) feature and specify a comma as the delimiter. This will correctly separate the values into columns.




This approach provides a simple and effective way to export aggregate results from LISSY, where users are not allowed to directly download files to a local storage folder. Instead, LISSY allows the download of job-related outputs such as the submitted code, the corresponding listings, and any generated visualizations (typically in image format).
Even in cases where personal storage is available, all outputs are subject to a disclosure control process: results must be reviewed and approved by LIS staff before they can be released to the user.
Within this context, exporting data via the console offers a practical workaround. By formatting aggregate results as CSV and copying them into a spreadsheet, users can quickly transfer structured data into external tools for further analysis, formatting, or presentation, without bypassing the platform’s safeguards.
